After testing six of these machines, we found ourselves rarely opening any manufacturer’s app simply to change a setting. Walking over and pressing the physical control was usually faster. For us, the most useful smart features are automatic operation and maintenance alerts rather than constant remote control. The InvisiClean isn’t the prettiest or fanciest model here, but its small footprint, quiet performance, and simplicity make it a practical compact choice.

Get the InvisiClean air purifier and humidifier at Amazon, Walmart, or InvisiClean.

Sources indicate that we’ve lived with the Blueair 2-in-1 Pro for more than a year and retested it alongside every model in this guide. It remains one of our favorite air-care appliances. At around $500, it’s undeniably expensive, but it’s still roughly half the price of the Dyson while delivering the larger capacity and performance we want for an open kitchen, dining room, or other substantial living space.

The design is particularly good. Like our Best Overall Blueair pick, the Pro looks more like intentionally chosen home decor than equipment you’d rather hide. Our favorite detail is the filling system: water can simply be poured into the top, where it gracefully passes through the unit into the reservoir below. It’s a small interaction, but it reflects how carefully Blueair seems to think about the everyday experience of using its products.

That attention extends to the controls, quiet operation, and overall build quality. After long-term use, this remains a machine we’re perfectly happy to keep prominently displayed in our kitchen and dining area. Dyson certainly has its own unmistakable design language, but we prefer Blueair’s more understated approach to modern technology. The Pro doesn’t shout for attention; it simply looks expensive, works exceptionally well, and integrates naturally into the room around it. For a larger space where both capacity and appearance matter, it’s the model we’d choose.

Get the Blueair Pro air purifier and humidifier at Amazon or Blueair.

We tested six air purifier and humidifier combinations for two months throughout a home, placing them in bedrooms, an office, a kitchen, and larger shared living areas. One model, the Blueair 2-in-1 Pro, had already been in long-term use for more than a year and was retested alongside the newer machines.

According to recent reports, we evaluated setup, controls and apps, humidification, purification response, noise, cleaning and refilling, and overall day-to-day usability. We also paid particular attention to automatic operation, noting how promptly each purifier responded when activities such as cooking or burning a candle changed surrounding air conditions. Since these are appliances many people leave visible and running continuously, design, reservoir access, maintenance, and how intrusive each unit felt during ordinary use also factored heavily into our scores and final awards.

Living with dry and unclean air can negatively affect comfort and health. Dry indoor air can cause an uncomfortable feeling at best and cracked skin at worst. Even “clean” indoor air can benefit from an air purifier, which can remove common pollutants such as pollen, pet hair, and smoke. Air purifying is even more key for allergy and asthma sufferers, who may notice a reduction in symptoms with a good air purifier.

Sources indicate that there is a difference between air purifier and humidifier units: Purifiers remove pollutants from air, whereas humidifiers add moisture to the air. Combination units do both. Consider the following factors when shopping for the best air humidifier and purifier: room size, filtration system, reservoir capacity, and additional user-friendly features.

Sources indicate that air humidifier and purifier combo units are intended for use in one room. (Whole-house humidifier and air purifier options are separate products and are usually professionally installed into the home’s climate control system.) For optimal performance, a unit should most often be used in a room that is the size of the manufacturer’s recommendation.

It’s possible to use a unit rated for a larger room in a smaller room, however, as long as a unit has a humidistat and auto-shutoff. The humidistat measures the ideal humidity, usually between 30 and 50 percent, and triggers the unit to shut off when ideal humidity is reached. Just know that if there’s no auto shut-off feature, a large humidifier can make a small room too humid.

While it’s crucial to take room size into account, the recommended room size can sometimes be misleading, so consider the CADR rating as well, explained ahead.

Industry observers note that air humidifiers and purifiers can have a few filter types, and many have a multistage filtration system. These systems can include activated carbon filters to remove odors, large particle filters, dust and pet hair filters, and the “gold standard,” HEPA (high-efficiency particulate air) filters. HEPA filters remove over 99.97 percent of dust mites, mold, pollen, bacteria, and other airborne particles measuring 0.3 microns (and actually trap smaller and larger particles even more effectively).

These extremely effective humidifiers with filters are shown to improve air quality. Shoppers who are interested in an air purifier and humidifier for allergies will want to look for a unit with a HEPA filter.

Sources indicate that air humidifiers and purifiers have a CADR (clean air delivery rate) score. This rating is used to measure an air purifier’s efficiency. It indicates the amount of filtered air a unit can deliver per minute and is often broken down into separate ratings for tobacco smoke, dust, and pollen. Products certified by the AHAM (Association of Home Appliance Manufacturers) are proven to live up to their CADR rating.

Sources indicate that the higher the CADR score, the faster the filtration system. CADR is often used to calculate the appropriate square footage for a unit. The AHAM recommends that the CADR score of a unit should be a minimum of two-thirds of the room’s square footage.

Some units don’t display a CADR score and only display the room size the unit is suitable for. Knowing the CADR score is more reliable, as some manufacturers will recommend a room size that does not align with the AHAM’s recommendations. According to the AHAM, the recommended room size should be based on 4.8 air changes per hour (how many times the purifier cleans and circulates the air in a room). Many manufacturers will share a recommended room size based on only one or two air changes per hour to boost their square footage recommendation.

Air humidifier purifier units have a reservoir to hold water, which the machine turns into moisture to release into the air. The unit’s overall size (and therefore reservoir size) often corresponds to its suited room size. Small units are usually ideal for small or medium-size rooms, but they may need more frequent refilling if they also have a small reservoir tank. Larger units will need less frequent topping up, but they’ll also take up more space.

Keep in mind that usage habits will also affect how often the water tank needs refilling. Many air humidifiers and purifiers have a water tank between a half gallon and 1 gallon, but extra-large options are also available—we’ve included one with a 3-gallon-plus capacity on this list.

Sources indicate that in our testing, reservoir design mattered almost as much as capacity. A slightly smaller tank that’s easy to remove, carry, and clean can be less frustrating than a larger reservoir with awkward access.

Industry observers note that daily cleaning and maintenance can ensure that your air cleaner humidifier operates correctly and does not emit any harmful particles into a space. Consumers are encouraged to use distilled water in their humidifiers and purifiers to reduce general maintenance and germ buildup. Wash and dry the humidifier after each use to remove any potential bacteria, mold, minerals, and chemicals.

Sources indicate that the Environmental Protection Agency advises using a 3 percent hydrogen peroxide solution to clean these machines every few days, clearing out any potential toxins. Finally, filters should be replaced as recommended by the manufacturer to ensure all contaminants are being removed.

According to recent reports, A good air humidifier and purifier should have a built-in humidistat that measures room humidity and adjusts operation accordingly. At minimum, the humidifier should shut off once the set humidity is reached to prevent the room from becoming overly damp.

Sources indicate that digital onboard controls are also useful, especially when they make it easy to adjust fan speed, humidity targets, and operating modes. Some models include a remote control for making changes from across the room.

In a recent development, smart models can connect to Wi-Fi and a smartphone app for monitoring air quality, setting schedules, and changing settings remotely. In our testing, however, we often found the physical controls faster for everyday adjustments. Apps were most useful for checking air-quality data and receiving maintenance alerts.

Filter-change and refill reminders are particularly helpful, whether they appear in an app or through indicator lights on the unit itself.

Choosing the best air humidifier and purifier for your home really comes down to choosing a user-friendly option that’s suitable for the intended room size. Still wondering if a combined purifier and humidifier is the right choice? Read on for some frequently asked questions and answers on room air purifiers and humidifiers to narrow down the best option for your needs.

No, air purifiers do not dry out a space’s air supply, especially when the machine includes a humidifier. These machines are designed to improve indoor air quality by removing particles, microorganisms, and gases.

Sources indicate that no—air purifiers trap mold and common allergen particles in the air, but not the mold spores that may be present somewhere in the home. To completely get rid of a mold problem, consider an effective mold remover.

It has been revealed that yes. Air purifiers and humidifiers perform different functions, so they can be used at the same time without interfering with each other. An air purifier filters airborne pollutants, while a humidifier adds moisture to dry air. In fact, combination units like the ones we tested are specifically designed to perform both jobs from the same location. Just avoid over-humidifying the room; aim to keep indoor humidity between about 30 and 50 percent.

Yes. Air purifiers are designed to be left on at all times. In fact, running an air purifier as often as possible is the most effective way to improve air quality. After all, indoor air quality is always changing depending on the air quality outside and what you do inside, like cooking, cleaning, or smoking. Leaving the air purifier on will help improve air quality, regardless of exterior factors.

In a way, yes. Stand-alone humidifiers don’t remove pollutants, but they do improve overall air quality by making the air feel more comfortable. Humidifiers can help keep indoor air humidity at an ideal level between 30 and 50 percent. Keeping indoor humidity in this sweet spot reduces the chance of mold growth and dust mites, which in turn can help maintain better air quality. To further improve air quality, look for a combined air purifier humidifier unit.

Sources indicate that no, not necessarily. A humidifier is useful if you struggle with dry indoor air. It’s not necessary (and can even be detrimental) to run a humidifier in humid homes. If the air in your home often dips beneath 30 percent, consider using a humidifier.

The unit needs to run for a certain length of time for you to take full advantage of the air purifier and humidifier benefits. Effectiveness depends on a wide range of factors, including the room size, the air purifier’s filtration system, the unit’s settings, and the surrounding humidity level. Consider the CADR rating and recommended room size to find a suitable unit. When these metrics are all taken into account, a good air purifier should create cleaner air in around just 15 minutes.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

Realtors weigh in on these common yard eyesores that can hurt curb appeal and make a home look less than its best.

What makes a yard an eyesore? It depends on who you ask. Like personal style and hygiene, everyone has different rules when it comes to yard upkeep and design. One person’s cherished garden gnomes might be another’s idea of tacky kitsch. Lawn decor might be a matter of taste, but neglected maintenance like a broken fence or rotting RV in the yard are harder to overlook.

The good news is that nobody has to agree on what makes one yard beautiful and another an eyesore (unless you live in an HOA!), but some yard features are bound to cause a head shake or two from the neighbors. Ahead, find some of the most controversial yard eyesores, with a reminder that curb appeal is always subjective.

Recent findings suggest that unmowed grass and overgrown weeds make a yard look neglected and can quickly crossover into eyesore territory. But that doesn’t mean everyone’s yard has to look perfectly manicured or exactly the same, either. “A yard that is basic is not a problem as long as it is well kept,” real estate broker Erik Leland says. “You could choose a meadow-style yard or a pollinator garden as long as it is intentional with defined paths and maintained edges.”.

It has been revealed that vibrant, healthy trees and shrubs add to a home’s curb appeal, but neglected, overgrown or dead ones can promptly tank it. Even if the rest of the yard is well-maintained, lifeless hedges and trees make it look like an eyesore. “Dead shrubs may appear minor. However, they create a larger perception glitch if the property owner is not maintaining something minor, like dead shrubs,” real estate agent Ben Mizes says.

In a recent development, broken or unused bulky items like patio furniture, piles of lumber, old furniture or broken lawn equipment can quickly pile up in the yard and become an eyesore. Difficult to dispose of, these items can overwhelm homeowners. “When you see clutter and junk in or around a home, it can create stress and uneasiness, even for neighbors,” Realtor Dell Jeanty states. “Keeping the yard organized can make the property and the entire street feel cleaner and more welcoming.”.

Industry observers note that fences can add to a home’s curb appeal and value, but a neglected one is just a yard eyesore. Broken, rotting and leaning fences drag down a property’s appeal and give the impression it’s not cared for. However, “a fence does not have to be upcoming to look good,” real estate expert Cameron Walker claims. “Old fences can be painted, and neglected and damaged fences can be repaired to make a good first impression.”.

In a recent development, adding statues and garden gnomes to your yard is a personal choice that not everyone will enjoy. What makes you smile may make your neighbor scratch their head. But, even if you are a fan, it is possible to have too much of a good thing. “The right amount of decorations can give personality to a yard and make it inviting, but too many can give a cluttered appearance,” Walker indicates. “Decorations should be placed to give ample space to display the landscaping.”.

According to recent reports, while low-maintenance artificial turf is appealing, it can look like an eyesore if not done correctly. Low-quality material and shoddy installation methods result in uneven seams and a cheap aesthetic. “One of the major problems is if it appears as if the grass has been glued to the ground,” Mizes says. But, even when done right, some people just don’t like the look of fake turf. It comes down to personal preference.

According to recent reports, A few carefully placed ornaments can give a yard character, but too many create an eyesore of visual clutter. “A property can lose appeal with an overabundance of various garden ornaments competing for focal points throughout the landscape,” Mizes says. “[But] a collection within a defined area of the landscape can be better appreciated.” Just know that your vision of a beautiful yard might look like a flea market to your neighbor.

“There’s nothing wrong with having garbage and recycling bins in the front yard during pick-up day, but leaving them lined up in front of the house all week doesn’t look great and robs the home of its curb appeal,” Jeanty says. “Tucking them beside the house or behind a small screen keeps the yard looking cleaner.” On the other hand, some folks just don’t see what the big deal is about hiding trash cans and that’s okay, too.

Broken down cars, ATVs or campers strewn in a yard qualify as a yard eyesore in most people’s eyes. Mice settle in, lawn and weeds grow around it and your property can start to resemble a junk yard. It knocks down your curb appeal and impacts your home’s value and your neighbor’s, too. A non-working vehicle doesn’t automatically constitute an eyesore, though, if it’s stored intentionally and preferably out of sight.

Recent findings suggest that while they may spread holiday cheer, not everyone cares for inflatable yard decorations. Where some see whimsy, others see tacky. No matter which side you’re on, most would agree that when deflated during the day, inflatables turn into a yard eyesore. “They just look like piles of plastic in your yard,” Leland says. Additionally, too many inflatables can be fun or make a yard look disorganized and cluttered, depending on your take.

Industry observers note that “A derelict shed or rotting play structure is sure to give a bad impression,” Leland notes. “If it’s not worth repairing, remove it. An empty space is the better choice.” When I moved into my current home, one of the first things we did was remove a large gazebo that was long past its prime. Our upcoming neighbors all came by and thanked us for removing the neighborhood eyesore.

Kitschy lawn ornaments like plastic flamingos could elicit an eye roll from a neighbor, but perhaps not. “A couple of plastic flamingos can be funny and add personality to a yard, so I wouldn’t automatically call them an eyesore,” Jeanty notes. “But when there are twenty of them with mismatched colors competing with signs, flags and other decorations, it becomes a little overwhelming.” Thoughtfully incorporate your outdoor decor into the landscape for a more tasteful display.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Given the attention his move has received, Yoo has written an op-ed for the Upcoming York Post explaining his decision to choose Texas, and disputing any suggestion that he was driven out of Berkeley.
  • I'm leaving not because I feel driven out by Berkeley — anything but.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Professor John Yoo is leaving the law school at the University of California at Berkeley to join the School of Civic Leadership at the University of Texas at Austin. As I noted here, his departure means there will not be a single right-leaning professor teaching public law subjects at Berkeley--and no more than a handful (if that) at all of the UC schools combined.

Given the attention his move has received, Yoo has written an op-ed for the Upcoming York Post explaining his decision to choose Texas, and disputing any suggestion that he was driven out of Berkeley.

I'm leaving not because I feel driven out by Berkeley — anything but.

In my three decades there I've enjoyed working, on an individual level, with spirited, ambitious students and challenging, innovative scholars.

I'm moving because Berkeley, like its peers, has declined from a daring, risk-taking center of higher learning to one that wallows contentedly in a monoculture of liberalism.

Yoo claims the school has been obsessed with ethnic diversity while disregarding viewpoint diversity, and that this has eroded the institution's commitment to free speech and created an environment in which anti-semitism has taken root.

I've watched students and the usual agitators disrupt debates on affirmative action, spark pitched fights on Sproul Plaza and try to shout down distinguished scholars and thinkers (home of the Free Speech Movement, indeed).

Tolerance of such shenanigans was matched by intolerance of conservative or libertarian views on the faculty.

Berkeley has consistently rejected conservative scholars, no matter how well-qualified, well-published or widely cited. . . .

Industry observers note that one famous member of a revered Berkeley humanities department (always ranked among the nation's top three) once told me directly that he would never hire a conservative. . . .

Most student groups at Berkeley Law now boycott any event with a speaker who believes in Israel's right to exist.

For the first time in my 33 years at Berkeley I witnessed a heckler's veto, as protesters prevented a member of the Israeli Knesset from speaking — and top university officials stood idly by.

Students posted flyers depicting the dean of the law school — a liberal scholar with whom I rarely agree — feasting on human beings, then physically invaded his home while he hosted members of the graduating class, simply because he is Jewish.

Yoo argues that great universities should refocus their teaching on Western Civilization, so that the nation does not lose sight of the ideals upon which it was founded and the principles that provide the foundation for western prosperity.

The emergence of human reason in Greece and religious revelation in Jerusalem produced the free markets, natural rights, rule of law and democratic self-government that have made our astounding prosperity and power possible.

According to recent reports, these ideals run directly counter to the poison running rampant on our campuses. . . .

Texas wants to restore Western civilization and the great books to the center of its curriculum — not to blindly agree with the past, but to understand and debate it.

I'm eager to join the Texans who want to defend free speech and thought, and to leave behind a California that rejects the West.

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

Your riding lawnmower can do double duty this winter by adding a snow plow. Here’s what you need to know before adding a plow to your riding mower.

Snow is considered a “four-letter” word in our home. Living in the northeast, right in the middle of the so called “I-95” corridor, we usually average 20 inches of snow a year. Even with my trusted 26-inch two-stage snow blower and my newest gadget, an 18 volt snow shovel, clearing the driveway and sidewalk can quickly turn into a significant time consuming and dangerous job. If you already own a riding mower (different from a lawn or garden tractor), you may wonder if you can add a snow plow to turn it into a useful piece of year-round equipment.

Industry observers note that the short answer is “yes, maybe,” said David Bodzioch, certified Small Engine and Automotive Technology Instructor. Snow (plow) blades are available for certain riding mowers. However, Bodzioch cautioned, “attaching a blade doesn’t necessarily make your mower ready to clean a snow-covered driveway.”.

Accessory compatibility, traction, mower size as well as the amount and type of snow you typically need to move will determine if you can, or should, add a plow blade to your riding lawnmower. Before investing in a plow, you need to understand what your mower can realistically handle. As well as determining what accessories you might need. Here’s what our experts have to say about turning a riding mower into a snow plow.

Sources indicate that “Yes, many riding lawnmowers can be equipped with a front-mounted snow blade,” noted certified Small Engine instructor Jeffrey Cesari. “Even if aftermarket compatible attachments are available, you should use the manufacturer’s approved attachments,” added Cesari. “Adding a plow blade on small tractors requires a set of rear wheel chains and a counterweight for balance,” added Cesari.

In a recent development, for example, John Deere sells a front blade package (as well as snow throwers) designed for specific riding lawnmowers. A John Deer 19 horsepower or better twin-cylinder engine units position the driver closer to the engine for better balance.

What Do You Need to Turn a Riding Lawnmower Into a Snow Plow?

Industry observers note that “At minimum, you’ll need a snow blade and direct-fit mounting hardware designed to fit your particular make and model mower,” said Bodzioch. Tire chains and weights should also be considered when operating snow-clearing equipment. According to Troy-Bilt, makers of outdoor power equipment, “Depending on the riding lawnmower mower and snow conditions, the mower will benefit from the added traction that chains and weights provide” when removing snow.

Recent findings suggest that “It depends on whether your mower simply requires a blade, or the added cost of mounting hardware, weights and tire chains,” said Cesari. An add on blade can cost as little as $120 for 22 to 32 inch width universal riding mower plow kit, to over $1400 for a complete John Deere 46 inch front blade snow plow package that includes an adjustable three-position blade height and angle setting you can change from the driver’s seat. Look for heavy-gauge steel blades that are height-adjustable and have the ability to reposition the shave plate for longer life.

Industry observers note that the biggest advantage is getting year-round use from expensive equipment you already own. Plus, eliminating the need for another piece of snow-removal equipment that sits unused for nine or ten months out of the year.

Recent findings suggest that “You’ll probably need to buy and install several accessories and that can be expensive,” stated Bodzioch. You should also check how difficult it is swapping out the snow blade and grass cutting mower deck. He added that “you also want check if your mower and blade combination are right for your type [concrete, blacktop, etc.] driveway.”.

Sources indicate that yes, it can be, and should be, as long as your mower is approved for the attachment, is well-maintained and in good working condition. Following the manufacturer’s operating, maintenance guides and safety instructions is mandatory for safe and efficient operation; the same as when using any other piece of outdoor power equipment.

Bodzioch stated, “Proper traction is especially key when driving on ice and snow, or on snow-covered grass or soil.” But Cesari also notes that “you need to be aware of frame structure and that adding a snow plow can cause frame damage, transmission wear and belt fatigue on small home riding mowers.” Cesari said plowing up to five inches should be safe. Always be cautious and use common sense if your mower is struggling while removing any amount of snow.

Sources indicate that it depends. It may only make sense if you already own a compatible mower. However, having room and space to safely store the blade should be a real consideration. Cesari added, “Converting your mower to a plow may require buying expensive attachments or accessories. Consider a standalone snow blower or a lawn/garden tractor if it’s difficult swap out the mower deck and plow.” If you regularly deal with challenging snow conditions, a dedicated snow-removal machine may be the better investment.

Sources indicate that it depends on how you use the word. While “riding mower” and “lawn tractor” are often interchangeable, there are key differences between the two pieces of equipment. A riding mower typically means any mower you sit on, including a lawn tractor or zero-turn mower. Nevertheless, a lawn/garden tractor will generally be more expensive and have a larger, sturdier frame. Lawn/garden tractors are designed and built to accept manufacturers’ compatible direct-fit attachments and accessories.

Sources indicate that A combination square pairs a sliding ruler with a head for checking 90- and 45-degree angles, measuring depths, and marking consistent offsets. Understanding squares, levels, and plumbs can help you compare different types of squares and their applications. Compact models suit small parts, while longer blades extend across wider workpieces. A combination square’s usefulness depends on the relationship between its blade and head. The blade should be straight, the graduations correctly spaced, and the working faces accurately set at 90 and 45 degrees. Fine scale divisions alone don’t establish accuracy; a detailed ruler cannot compensate for an out-of-square head.

Sources indicate that check a new square before relying on it. Register the head against a known straight edge, draw a fine line, then flip the square and draw again from the same point. Diverging lines indicate a problem. Keep contact surfaces free of debris, and repeat the check after a drop or impact that could affect alignment.

According to recent reports, look for a blade with crisp, easy-to-read markings in the units and increments you use most. If you’re more familiar with metrics, you’ll want to choose millimeter markings.

Squares with etched markings tend to be more expensive, but they also hold up better than printed markings that can wear off with repeated handling. Dark markings on satin-finished blades can be easier to read under bright shop lights.

For reliable combination square use, the blade should slide smoothly when the lock is loosened and remain fixed when tightened. Binding makes small adjustments frustrating, while excessive play can prevent the blade from seating consistently. Check that the head sits firmly against the workpiece without rocking and that the adjustment knob is easy to grip.

A combination square is a measuring and layout tool with a ruler that slides through an adjustable head. The standard head provides 90- and 45-degree working faces, allowing the tool to check corners, mark miters, and measure depths or offsets.

According to recent reports, rest the head firmly against a workpiece’s edge to mark or check 90- and 45-degree angles. Slide and lock the blade to measure depths, check heights, or mark consistent offsets. The removable blade also serves as a ruler. Accuracy varies by model and manufacturing tolerances. A straight blade, accurately machined head, and secure lock all contribute to reliable results. Fine graduations don’t guarantee accuracy, and price alone doesn’t establish it. Check any newly introduced square before use and recheck it after a drop or impact.

Use a board with a known straight edge. Hold the square’s head firmly against that edge and draw a fine line along the blade. Flip the square, register the head against the same edge, and align the blade with the line’s starting point. Draw again. The lines should coincide; any divergence indicates a squareness error, assuming the board’s edge is straight and the tool is seated correctly.

In a recent development, to set the blade, loosen the locking knob, slide it to the desired measurement, and retighten. If the square appears inaccurate, remove the blade, clean its groove and the head’s contact surfaces, then reassemble and repeat the accuracy check.Calibration procedures vary by design. Some squares permit correction at the blade’s seating surfaces, but filing or sanding removes material permanently and can worsen the error. Follow the manufacturer’s instructions or seek service or replacement if cleaning doesn’t resolve the problem.

In a recent development, wipe away dust, moisture, and debris after use, paying particular attention to the blade groove and locking mechanism. Dry the tool before storing it, and apply any lubricant or rust protection according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Avoid abrasives on the graduations and measuring faces. Store the square where its blade won’t bend, and protect the head from drops and impacts.

As you think about how high to mount a TV, most experts use the center of the TV screen as the main point of reference, no matter the screen size. Forty-two inches from the floor to the center of the screen is the ideal TV mount height under most circumstances.

You’ll find a more exact center point for your TV mount by measuring the distance from the floor to each household member’s eye level when sitting. Add those measurements together and divide by the total number of people for your bespoke TV wall mount height.

Note that while TV size doesn’t always affect mounting height, a TV’s dimensions matter when considering optimal viewing distance. Recent findings suggest that everyone recognizes an emergency siren. Or do they?

Officers can choose different tones to make their vehicles easier to notice on busy streets or open roads. Some departments also use certain sounds for special warnings. With electronic siren systems offering several options, drivers might hear multiple tones during a single emergency response.

Learn what the common sounds mean, why officers switch between them, whether different tones signal different emergencies, and how drivers should react.

Different police siren sounds serve different purposes, but they don’t necessarily indicate specific emergencies. Officers often switch tones based on traffic conditions or to get drivers’ attention. A faster siren doesn’t always mean a more serious emergency.

Recent findings suggest that modern police vehicles typically use electronic sirens that allow officers to switch between these sounds. Older mechanical sirens use a spinning mechanism to produce a traditional wail.

Departments set their own policies for siren use, so there isn’t one standard sound for daytime or nighttime driving.

Regardless of the siren sound, drivers should respond the same way when an emergency vehicle approaches. Drivers should check their mirrors, signal, and safely pull toward the right side of the road to let the police vehicle pass. They should avoid sudden braking or stopping in an intersection.

Sources indicate that anyone already in an intersection should continue through before pulling over. Drivers waiting at a red light shouldn’t enter the intersection unless an officer directs them to do so. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last week, Professor Mark W. Smith released his newly introduced 85-minute film discussing the operations and mechanics of modern firearms, including semiautomatic rifles such as the popular AR-15 rifle. The film, titled "Firearms and the AR-15 Rifle: A Primer for the Bench and Bar," can be found on YouTube here and on Rumble. It has already been viewed over 23,000 times since its release only days ago. The film is broken down into 25 segments so a viewer can jump from topic to topic.

That federal judges are now reviewing Internet videos to learn about firearms is hardly surprising. A few weeks ago Judge Doris Pryor of the Seventh Circuit made reference to this during oral argument in a constitutional fight over the legality of Illinois's suppressor ban. In the consolidated cases of Anderson v. Raoul and Morse v. Raoul, argued October 28, 2026, she acknowledged that she has watched videos in preparing for oral argument. The oral argument audio recording is here with Judge Pryor's comment at the 25:04-25:23 mark.

As I previously wrote, I had the pleasure of introducing the "AR-15 Primer" film. From there, Rick Vasquez (a former ATF firearm technician and U.S. Marine ordnance officer) takes the spotlight explaining the mechanical operation of today's AR-15 rifle and its typical features.

But there is another important aspect of the film that is worth noting. And that is the impressive animations found within the film that help educate legal professionals and the general public about the internal and related operations of the AR-15 (and most modern semi-automatic rifles).

The animations found throughout the film are informative for those learning about firearm mechanics. Here are a few of the noteworthy ones:.

There is an excellent 2-minute animation illustrating how gas-operated semiautomatic rifles internally deploy the rapidly-expanding gases from the firing of a shot to do two things: first, to send a projectile (the bullet) down the barrel and, second, to prepare the rifle to fire the next round of ammunition. This is called autoloading. This dual use of the gases from firing a single shot is generally not understood or appreciated by those newly introduced to firearms technology, but the film's animation makes it clear. This animation also clarifies that autoloading does not mean automatic fire (like one sees with a M16 machine gun). The animation can be seen at the 14:58 to 17:58 mark of the film.

The film also does a nice job demonstrating the physical reality of recoil by illustrating how the features of an AR-15 like the straight line stock, the buffer spring/buffer tube, and the muzzle brake help to minimize recoil allowing for a more comfortable and effective shooting experience. The 28:09 to 28:22 mark has a nice illustration of the straight-line stock while the 28:28 to 28:59 mark illustrates the role of the buffer and buffer spring in minimizing uncomfortable recoil. The 27:59 to 28:07 mark shows an animation illustrating what constitutes recoil from the firing of a rifle.

According to recent reports, the film also effectively uses animation to illustrate the difference between scopes, red dot optics, and iron sights. A scope magnifies the target making it appear closer than it really is; a red dot optic helps the user aim the rifle using an electronic dot without magnification; and iron sights entail aligning a front post with a rear sight. The 1:00:53 to 1:01:18 mark illustrates these differences.

In a recent development, animation also helps viewers understand that the barrel of a semiautomatic rifle gets hot when the rifle is fired due to the internal gas explosion that results from firing a round. The film's animation shows the rifle barrel heating up and demonstrates the value of handguards (often called "barrel shrouds" in legislation) to protect the user of the rifle. The 46:24 to 46:33 mark illustrates a barrel heating up as the rifle is shot.

According to recent reports, the film's use of animations to explain the difference between a bullet and a cartridge is also worth mentioning. Lawyers (and even some judges) use those terms interchangeably, but they mean very different things. The 1:10:12 to 1:11:08 mark illustrates the four components (primer, gun power, case and bullet) of a modern ammunition cartridge.

According to recent reports, it has been said that the late President Harry Truman embraced the thought, "I am from Missouri so you have to show me." Well, Professor Smith's upcoming film on firearm mechanics works hard to "show" (through animations, illustrations and images) the internal mechanics and features of AR-15 semiautomatic rifles. And I suspect the bench and the bar will be the better for it.

Set up a portable unit outside your home, and connect appliances inside to its numerous outlets via extension cords. Exactly how many appliances it’ll power at once depends on the wattage that generator can handle.

In a recent development, while a portable generator might cost several hundred or even thousands of dollars depending on size and model, when compared to a standby generator, which would kick on automatically to power your home, it’s certainly less expensive. Plus, you may not need a professional electrician to install a portable generator, and you can easily take the unit with you should you move. All that said, proper operation of the machine is crucial to ensure the safety of your family and your community.

Before you start up a portable generator, bear in mind these two essential considerations:.

WEN’s 5600-watt generator has a push-button start and is powerful enough to run household essentials; noise level is about 88 dB. Read the review.

Because portable gas generators emit carbon monoxide while they’re running and for some time afterward, positioning the generator properly and practicing careful carbon monoxide safety is critical.

Before you start up the generator, check the fuel gauge and fill the tank with gasoline as needed. (Make sure the generator is on a level surface to get an accurate reading on the fuel gauge.) If you need to add fuel, consult the owner’s manual for fuel requirements.

Next, check the oil level, which is like checking the oil in your car. Locate the oil dipstick (often below a removable maintenance panel). Pull out the dipstick, wipe it off, and then re-insert it. Carefully pull the dipstick straight out once more, then look to see if the oil on the stick falls between the lower and upper limit marks imprinted on the dipstick. Add or change the oil if necessary, referring to your owner’s manual for how to add, what kind to use, and how frequently it needs to be changed.

Before plugging in, ensure that you won’t overload the generator by connecting more appliances and lights than it is rated to handle. Add up the starting and running wattage of the appliances you want to power simultaneously; refer to their respective user manuals or check the backs or sides of the machines to find this information. The total number should not exceed the wattage limitations of your generator. Check your user’s manual if you’re unsure of how many watts of power your generator can handle. Stagger the use of appliances if necessary to prevent overloading the generator.

It has been revealed that follow your user manual for instructions on turning on the machine. You typically will need to turn the circuit breaker off and turn the fuel valve on before starting it up. Give the machine a few minutes to warm up, then flip the circuit breaker on.

Sources indicate that use long, heavy-duty extension cords made for outdoor use to connect appliances to the generator one by one so as not to overload it. Examine cords before use to ensure they are in good condition with no rips or tears. The cord’s wattage rating should be greater than the wattage of what you’ve plugged into it.

Recent findings suggest that to shut down the generator, turn off or disconnect the appliances plugged into it. Then refer to your user’s manual to power down the generator—typically you’ll need to turn the circuit breaker, engine switch, and fuel valve to the “off” position.

Wait until the generator is completely cooled down before storing it once power is restored. If you don’t anticipate needing it again for more than a month, drain the fuel and carburetor. Leaving old fuel can damage the generator’s internal parts. Refer to your owner’s manual for storage instructions.

Industry observers note that when running a portable generator, safety is the name of the game. Keep these tips in mind before, during, and after use.

Industry observers note that maintaining healthy indoor air quality is essential for protecting members of your household from hidden carcinogens, allergens, and harmful particulates. Pollutants can enter your living space from a range of sources, including building materials that emit volatile organic compounds (VOCs) and poor ventilation that traps moisture and encourages mold growth.

In a recent development, while clues like window condensation, musty odors, or unexplained respiratory symptoms can signal trouble, invisible, odorless threats such as radon and carbon monoxide often go undetected without the right equipment. We spoke to indoor air quality experts to identify the top five indoor air pollutants in U.S. homes and how to fix or mitigate them.

This monitor impressed our product testers with accurate readings, and it connects to an app where owners can find air quality reports for their home.

Recent findings suggest that particulate matter—including tiny airborne particles like pollen, smoke, soot, and other debris—is one of the most common indoor air pollutants, notes Dr. Jaspreet Dhau, an expert on indoor air quality and purification and vice president of research and development at Molekule in Palm Beach Gardens, Florida. “Fine particulate matter, particularly PM2.5, which is a particle measuring 2.5 microns [micrometers] or smaller, is a concern because it can travel deep into the respiratory system,” says Dhau. Common sources include cooking, burning candles, using a fireplace, vacuuming, and even opening windows when outdoor pollution levels are high.

VOCs are gases released by certain household products and materials such as paint, solvents, flooring, furniture, adhesives, cleaning supplies, air fresheners, and personal care products. “VOC levels may be higher during and after a home renovation, when upcoming furniture is brought into a home, or when products containing chemical ingredients are used without adequate ventilation,” states Dhau. For example, certain pressed wood furniture and building materials can release formaldehyde, he explains.

Carbon monoxide (CO) is a combustion byproduct, a pollutant released when something burns. “In a typical home, sources can include gas stoves, fireplaces, wood-burning stoves, furnaces, water heaters, candles, and tobacco products,” indicates Dhau. “Carbon monoxide is especially dangerous because it’s colorless and odorless, making it difficult to detect without a working CO alarm.”.

In a recent development, biological contaminants such as dust mites and pet dander are airborne pollutants that originate from living organisms, states Dhau. “Dust mites are a frequent problem and tend to collect in mattresses, carpets, upholstered furniture, and bedding. They can enter homes through open windows, pets, clothing, and HVAC systems,” he explains. Signs you might have a problem include frequent dust buildup on surfaces, allergy symptoms, excess pet hair and dander, and dust accumulating around air vents, adds Bill Myers, indoor air quality expert and group manager for technical sales at Panasonic Eco Systems North America.

Quiet, effective and easy to use, this commercial-grade unit cleans the air with a washable pre-filter, a carbon filter, and a HEPA filter.

Industry observers note that everyday activities such as cooking and showering introduce moisture into the home. “When excess moisture is not adequately removed, particularly in bathrooms, basements, and other low-ventilation areas, conditions can become more favorable for mold and mildew growth,” notes Meyers. You might notice foggy mirrors that take a long time to clear, condensation on windows, musty odors, bathrooms that remain damp long after use, and visible mold or mildew.

Power outages are top of mind now more than ever before—and for good reason. One in four households experience a power outage in a year, according to U.S. Census Bureau data, and 70 percent of those reporting outages were without power for 6 hours or more. These longer outages are not only disruptive; they can also be expensive, considering that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration recommends tossing perishable food kept in the refrigerator after just 4 hours without power.

It has been revealed that backup power promises comfort and security, which is why so many homes rely on a portable generator or power station. That category has grown from gas-powered generators to multi-fuel units, portable power stations, and whole-home batteries. The newest member of the family? A fridge backup.

Sources indicate that just in 2026, this latest style hard-rolled out with models from three industry leaders: Bluetti’s Fridge Power, Jackery’s FridgeGuard, and Backup Core by BioLite. And the consumer response has been powerful. Bluetti’s Kickstarter hit 145 percent of its funding goal in 45 days. Jackery debuted as a Costco exclusive in June and expanded its retail distribution after hearing about customers carrying home multiple units. BioLite has released its Backup in two waves already, each selling out in weeks, and is taking orders now for January shipments. Clearly, homeowners want a backup built just for the fridge. Keep reading to learn more about what sets fridge backups apart and when one beats a generator.

Fridge-optimized batteries all share three main hallmarks:.

Think of it like a larger version of the uninterruptible power supply (UPS) that you might use in a home office or with a high-end entertainment center to keep your connected electronics running during a brownout or blackout. A UPS in the home office might offer surge protection and enough battery life to run your computer for another 5 minutes so you can safely shut it down; this fridge-optimized backup can keep your most important kitchen appliance on for 15 hours or more.

And while we call them “fridge” backups, the design is actually much more versatile. Plug them in and slip the slim backups easily into any room to keep an important appliance operational for hours: under a bed to power a CPAP machine, behind a bookshelf within cord’s reach of an air purifier, or behind the fish tank to maintain the family pet’s habitat.

Recent findings suggest that kickstarter backers for the Backup by BioLite—which first debuted in 2024 on the crowdfunding platform—“got it” immediately. “They understood the problem it was solving, and most questions revolved around understanding additional applications and setups beyond the fridge because the kitchen application was so intuitive,” indicates Erica Rosen, the VP of Marketing at BioLite and Goal Zero brands. “For example, we got a lot of questions about sump pumps and if Backup could run one during an outage.” (Spoiler alert: It can.).

Today, homeowners (and renters!) have many options for backup power, each with its own set of pros and cons.

A standby generator or whole-home battery backup automatically kicks in to keep the essentials—if not the whole home—running during an outage. Each type of backup connects at the electrical panel with a transfer switch. As such, each is a larger investment (read: more expensive) and a permanent installation that requires a licensed electrician. These backups also require forethought about fuel. A standby generator will require a source of liquid propane and/or natural gas, whereas whole-home batteries are often charged from the grid before an event and potentially recharged via solar panels when the grid is down.

Industry observers note that A portable gas-powered generator is more affordable than a standby option, but should only be run outdoors, which creates some limitations. For starters, you need to be home to turn a portable generator on and connect to your appliance. Then, you’ll need a long, heavy-duty outdoor-rated extension cord to reach the kitchen. These generators operate loudly, emit exhaust fumes, and require you to store enough fuel to be ready for the worst. Assuming you have a good supply, though, you can keep your appliance(s) powered with minimal interruption using a reliable portable generator.

Recent findings suggest that A power station brings backup power indoors to power multiple electronics and small appliances. Power stations are the closest comparison. They are safe to use indoors or out and feature similar battery capacities. You can find options in the ballpark of 1 to 2 kWh for similar price points. They can, but may not always be, plugged in 100 percent of the time to act as a UPS. And importantly, they’re often too bulky to leave out next to a refrigerator 24/7.

Sources indicate that A fridge backup offers instant power backup without a permanent installation. It’s ideal for the consumer who is looking for a user-friendly, set-and-forget setup and a safety net that offers enough power to keep a fridge running for approximately 15 hours while the power is out—longer if additional batteries are connected.

“It’s [designed for] someone who wants peace of mind without having to think too much about backup power. Maybe you live somewhere with frequent storms, or you’ve come home after an outage to find everything in your freezer has spoiled,” indicates Beau Tyrrel, Product Manager at Jackery. “It’s also useful for renters and those who live in apartments and can’t install a whole-home backup system. All you need is a standard outlet, and you can take it with you when you move.”.

Industry observers note that the design is appealing in more ways than one, notes Luna Yan, affiliate marketing manager at Bluetti. A fridge backup solves spatial problems that come with more traditional portable power stations: “Traditional backup power systems are often bulky, making them difficult to accommodate in homes with limited space, particularly in kitchens and apartments.”.

Recent findings suggest that “When we set out to develop Backup, we knew the world didn’t need another box-format power station. We did a lot of user research and found that there was a meaningful gap between the power stations of the world and expensive whole-home backup solutions, and it was leaving a lot of people out of the resiliency conversation,” Rosen says. “As we explored ways to answer this, it became clear that form factor was going to be a really important element: If we wanted something plugged in permanently to enable automatic performance, it needed to be really easy and it could not take up precious living space.”.

Industry observers note that it’s especially useful if you’re away when the power goes out and can’t move the fridge’s plug to a generator. Already plugged into the wall from setup, the backup’s stored power will be usable immediately. Each model’s mobile app demonstrates outage alerts, battery level, and power draw from anywhere.

Recent findings suggest that “[A fridge backup is] also useful for renters and those who live in apartments and can’t install a whole-home backup system. All you need is a standard outlet, and you can take it with you when you move.”.

Sources indicate that there’s a cost to every power outage. One of the biggest concerns for most homeowners is the spoiled food in a refrigerator after 4 hours without power. “Refrigerators are one of the few appliances in your home that needs to run around the clock,” Tyrrel notes. “When the power goes out, you could lose hundreds of dollars in groceries.”.

A blackout can cost the average American household $117 in spoiled groceries, according to a survey of more than 1,000 Americans by the Texas electric provider Payless Power. One in five homes had it worse, losing more than $200 in groceries during a single outage.

It has been revealed that using that average, we estimate that a $1,000 fridge backup pays for itself after 10 blackouts—potentially sooner in larger households or homes with especially packed fridges and freezers. For an area that experiences one to two extended blackouts in a year, this investment could earn its keep in as soon as 6 years—and these latest backups are rated for 10 or more years of use.

“Based on customer feedback, refrigerators are among the most notable appliances to keep running during a power outage,” Yan notes. And for good reason: “Continuous refrigeration helps protect food, medications, and other temperature-sensitive items.”.

In a recent development, if your utility firm offers a Time-of-Use (TOU) electricity pricing proposal, any of these fridge backups can help you take advantage of the savings. TOU programs charge different supply rates based on when you use electricity, incentivizing customers to use more electricity when overall demand is low by charging less per kilowatt-hour (kWh) used. These “off-peak hours” vary by plan, but typically are overnight and early morning.

For the average homeowner, the main way to save on these plans is to optimize the electricity usage you can schedule: when you charge an electric vehicle, run the dishwasher, and wash or dry a load of laundry. A fridge, of course, runs all day, and an efficient, Energy Star-certified model can use anywhere from 358 kWh for a compact top-freezer unit to 805 kWh per year for a large side-by-side refrigerator. You can’t optimize the always-on appliance without either a whole-home power bank that recharges in an off-peak hour for use during peak times or, now, a fridge backup. In a connected mobile app, users specify the best times to charge (off-peak hours) and discharge (peak hours), effectively shifting the fridge’s grid use to cheaper hours.

Especially now, with rising concern about grid stability and the increasing frequency of natural disaster events that disrupt power, demand for energy backups is high. Each of these energy brands has sold out and replenished stock at least once already this year. So while you may be eager to set up your home with the first available fridge backup, here’s a comprehensive look at unit specs to help find the model best suited to your space and needs.

Bluetti’s fridge backup offers the largest base capacity—nearly double that of Jackery FridgeGuard, and expandable to 8 kWh (second only to BioLite’s 10.5 kWh). Divide the total cost by the capacity, and you’re paying about $470 per kWh, which is the most backup per dollar. One unit can power the typical modern fridge for 21 to 48 hours, and a maximized setup of FridgePower plus three BlueCell battery packs can power your fridge for 4 days. (Run time, of course, depends on the specific refrigerator’s energy consumption and usage conditions.) That makes the slim design even more impressive—though at 43 pounds, it’s a two-person job to wall-mount.

The mobile app provides battery levels, outage status, and charging progress, plus a place to choose among four UPS modes: Standard, PV Priority (which prioritizes solar power), TOU (Time-of-Use), and Custom. It even tracks local weather, alerts you when a storm approaches, and switches to fast charging if needed. An optional magnetic display (sold separately) provides at-a-glance information including percentage charged, energy output, and UPS modes—all without opening your phone.

Recent findings suggest that on paper, the Jackery fridge backup appears to be the unit most specialized for fridge use. It offers up to 15 hours of power in the slimmest profile. One outlet (for the fridge) and a single expansion option make it the least flexible of the three—but if the fridge is all you need, it’s a perfect fit. It’s effective, affordable, lasts up to 16 years, and takes only one person to install the lightweight unit on a wall mount (sold separately). It offers surge protection for your most key household appliance during voltage spikes and enough power to start the fridge.

One distinction Jackery has over its competition is a choice between instant backup UPS and a delayed start. “Your refrigerator’s compressor needs a little time to recover,” Tyrrel explains. “When it stops, refrigerant pressure remains high on one side of the system. Restarting too quickly makes the motor work harder and briefly draw several times its normal current. Delayed Start gives the compressor a short pause before restarting, helping avoid unnecessary strain when power flickers on and off.”.

It has been revealed that from the moment an outage occurs, Backup Core automatically powers a refrigerator for 15 to 30 hours. At 29 inches long, it’s 5 to 6 inches longer than all of the other units, but rotating it can fit one atop even a fridge and its slim design should still slip behind the appliance on its vertical wall mount.

In a recent development, given its size and expansion capabilities, it should come as no surprise that Backup Core also includes the most outlets for electronics. Whereas another model includes one or two ports on the unit, the forward-thinking BioLite design provides its own power strip—that’s three more openings for small kitchen appliances or other electronics to easily connect.

Sources indicate that bioLite’s Backup Core is a 1.5 kWh solution, similar to its sister brand Goal Zero Yeti 1500 (6th generation). “However, Backup can expand in 1.5kWh increments with the ‘Extend’ model, and chain up to 10.5kWh of localized capacity,” Rosen explains. That’s even more than the combined 8kWh capacity of the Yeti Pro 4000 and Yeti Pro Tank 4000. So while Backup Core is the priciest of the three, it’s also the only one that can grow into something close to a whole-home battery. Think of it less as a fridge backup and more as the first piece of a backup system.

Before or After the Snow? Here’s the Right Time to Salt Your Driveway This Winter

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that the Centers for Disease Control report a 35 percent increase in outdoor slips and falls during the winter months.
  • Industry observers note that it depends.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

Salt your driveway like a pro this winter with these expert-backed tips.

Recent findings suggest that the Centers for Disease Control report a 35 percent increase in outdoor slips and falls during the winter months. Icy sidewalks, stairs and driveways are largely to blame for this seasonal uptick. Icy driveways are not only dangerous to walk on but also make driving and parking difficult. Ice melt salt is one of the best ways to keep driveways clear, but how should you best use it? Should you apply it before or after a storm — or both? Two industry experts weigh in on the best way to salt your driveway for optimal results this winter.

Industry observers note that it depends. Salting before a big storm with heavy snow and ice accumulation is a good idea, but timing matters.

Plan to apply salt several hours before a storm hits for best results. It creates a salty coating that prevents the initial snowfall from bonding with the driveway surface. Pre-salting reduces total snow accumulation and makes snow removal easier once the storm is over. Avoid doing it too far in advance, or if rain is in the forecast, as the salt can be washed or blown away before the snow arrives. It’s not necessary to salt before a light snowfall of less than six inches.

It’s always a good idea to salt after it snows, but don’t rely on it to replace snow removal efforts. First remove as much snow as possible with a shovel or snowblower, then use salt to clear away any remaining slush and snow.

The best time to salt is immediately after snow removal, before cold nighttime temperatures set in. “When applied before the temperatures drop, salt prevents ice from forming and ensures the snow does not freeze solid to the ground,” Angelika Klimorowski, a winter maintenance specialist at Online Rock Salt, notes.

Apply salt before and after a big storm for best results, especially when heavy snow, sleet or freezing rain is expected.

In a recent development, “Pre-salting helps prevent ice from bonding to the driveway, while a second application can help break down any ice that forms,” Aaron Strickland, owner of Mr. Trim Lawn & Garden Services, says. “For a typical snowfall, both applications usually aren’t necessary.”.

If only a few inches of snow is forecast, salting after snow removal is likely sufficient. Applying salt before and after a small storm is not only a waste of money, but can damage driveway surfaces, burn lawn edges and generate harmful storm runoff.

“The exact amount of rock salt that you need will depend on how big the area is that you are planning to de-ice,” Klimorowski indicates. A little goes a long way, and more is not better. A 12-oz. coffee mug filled with salt is enough to treat a 1,000-sq.-ft. driveway. Spread salt evenly, leaving about 3 inches between salt grains. Avoid overapplication, as it can degrade driveway surfaces and harm the environment.

A handheld spreader makes application easier and more consistent, especially for larger driveways. “We try to follow recommended coverage rates and use a spreader wherever possible,” Strickland indicates. “Too much salt wastes product and can damage surrounding grass and gardens.” If spreading salt by hand, always wear gloves and cascade it for even coverage.

Rock salt is only effective down to ground temperatures of 15 to 17 degrees. Don’t apply more salt if it’s not working, as it’s likely too cold out for it to work. “If your area tends to experience colder temperatures, you may need to find an alternative de-icing product to keep your surfaces safe,” Klimorowski claims. Calcium chloride and magnesium chloride ice melt products are two common alternatives that remain effective at sub-zero temperatures.

Yes, rain will wash away salt rather than dissolve it. It then ends up in storm drains and potentially pollutes local bodies of water.

Rock salt stops working in temperatures below 10 to 15 degrees.

“While it is true that salt will work best if you apply it before the temperatures drop, there is no deadline, and you can always apply it later,” Klimorowski says.

Recent findings suggest that there’s no guarantee salt will damage your driveway, but you should use it sparingly. Concrete driveways are particularly vulnerable to salt damage.

We selected and tested a diverse assortment of waterproof gloves designed for a variety of uses in different seasons. On those gloves not listed as unisex, women tested women’s gloves, and men tested men’s gloves.

First, we simulated storm conditions with a rain-wand attachment on a garden hose. The testers wore each pair of gloves beneath a steady 2-minute shower, flexing their hands and turning them over to expose all parts of the gloves to the stream. In the second test, we immersed our gloved hands into a bucket of water, again flexing and rotating to ensure that they were completely wet. Finally, we tested them for wet-gripping ability while handling smooth wet stones. To merit inclusion in this guide, each pair of gloves passed all three tests with minimal water intrusion to the inside of the glove.

According to recent reports, before shopping for the best waterproof gloves, consider the type of work planned for the gloves as well as the kind of materials and construction desired. In this section, we review some key considerations to keep in mind while shopping for the best waterproof gloves, including materials, use, fit, and more.

Choosing the best waterproof gloves depends on how they’ll be used. Work gloves are completely different from those intended for outdoor sports or casual wear.

On garments labeled “waterproof,” the outer shell is usually where the magic happens. Materials like tightly woven nylon, polyester, softshell technical materials, treated leather, and others work well to shed water before it can seep through to the lining. Keep in mind that it’s very rare for leather gloves to actually be waterproof; more likely, they are simply water-resistant.

Aside from shell material, other elements in waterproof gloves’ exteriors make them useful in wet or messy situations. Some of the best waterproof gloves, for example, have textured grips that make it easier for the wearer to grab on to wet, slippery surfaces, making them ideal for skiing, cycling, and other active pursuits. Those looking for waterproof gloves for work may want to invest in gloves with reinforced palms and thumbs, which should last longer and stand up to more wear.

The best waterproof gloves contain an optional outer shell with conductors that transfer the electrical charge from a finger to a touch screen, allowing consumers to manipulate their phones without removing their gloves.

Industry observers note that some of the best waterproof gloves contain insulation that captures body heat, which forms air pockets that warm with the heat from the hand. Most insulation is a man-made poly-fill material such as Thinsulate or 3M.

According to recent reports, to ensure gloves keep warm air inside and cold air from seeping in, some waterproof gloves have long elastic cuffs that hug tight to the wrist and arm, closing off any pathway for air to enter. For even warmer gloves, look for removable liners that can slip inside a waterproof glove to add another layer of insulation.

Sources indicate that when selecting the best waterproof gloves, fit and comfort are essential. However, a “good fit” is relative to the activity. A pair of running gloves fits quite differently than a pair of winter work gloves or ski gloves.

Waterproof running or hiking gloves often feel like a stretchy, flexible second skin. Because they’re lightweight and wick away moisture, owners sometimes forget they’re even wearing them.

According to recent reports, waterproof work gloves are bulkier and a bit stiff because they’re generally made from thick nylon or leather that resists ripping, tearing, and friction. Moreover, extra padding or reinforcement on the thumbs or palms can add to their bulk. Though work gloves fit loosely, they shouldn’t be so loose that it’s difficult to pick up small items while wearing them.

Ski gloves are flexible but don’t wear particularly well because they’re typically made from materials like nylon. Properly fitting ski gloves fit snugly around the wrist but are roomy enough to allow the skier to manipulate straps on ski poles and boot bindings.

Industry observers note that also consider breathability. If hands sweat and moisture collects inside the glove, it won’t matter that the shell is waterproof because hands will still get wet. Breathable gloves help some of the heat and moisture escape without letting in cold outer air and moisture.

How to Shovel the Trickiest Surfaces the Right Way, From Pavers to Your Roof

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that clearing snow from walkways is vital for safety, but winter shoveling can easily damage wooden decks, asphalt driveways and other surfaces.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

From lawns to sealed concrete, you might be surprised at how much damage a snow shovel can do.

Recent findings suggest that clearing snow from walkways is vital for safety, but winter shoveling can easily damage wooden decks, asphalt driveways and other surfaces. So, as the days get shorter and colder, it’s vital to solidify your shoveling blueprint before the first snow flies.

In a recent development, “Snow can camouflage uneven areas and patches of ice, posing slip-and-fall risks, particularly when you’re rushing to shovel,” claims landscaping expert Jose Lopez. “Being mindful and taking a relaxed, careful approach will help you save money and keep everyone safe all winter long.”.

Ahead, experts walk through how to shovel eleven tricky surfaces around your home, to keep everyone safe, plus prevent costly springtime repairs.

According to recent reports, shoveling gravel is frustrating because those pebbles tend to come up with the snow, then get scattered onto the landscaping. “You will end up cleaning about $150 worth of it off your lawn in the spring,” claims grading and paving contractor Scott Flores.

To make life easier, use a plastic shovel, keep the blade about an inch above the gravel and clear the snow in short passes. “You don’t have to expose all of the gravel,” claims Lopez. “It’s fine to leave a thin layer of snow behind.”.

Industry observers note that A metal snow shovel blade can actually scratch and gouge concrete. “It can cause $3,000 worth of damage to your pavement in 20 minutes and you won’t know it ’til April,” notes Flores. Initially, the damage “may not look like much, but once water gets under it and freezes, it will cause spalling and make your pavement look 10 years older than it is.”.

Luckily, the fix is easy on this one: always use a poly-blade (plastic) or rubber-edged shovel on concrete.

Aliaksandr Bahdanovich/Getty Images.

Aggressive shoveling can damage paint and sealers, even if they’re touted as “scratch-resistant.” “That layer is about three millimeters thick, and your steel shovel will chip it away like you’re peeling your fingernails,” notes Flores.

The fix: use a poly-blade shovel, shovel with a slight upward motion and leave a half-inch of snow for the sun to melt, indicates Flores. “Many believe that steel shovels will last longer. Yes they will, but that’s what makes them bad,” he says.

Pro-tip: If you use a deicer, make sure it’s safe for your particular coating, says Lopez.

It has been revealed that just like with concrete, asphalt seems indestructible, but metal shovels can damage it, especially if it already has imperfections or cracks. So, the best approach is to use a poly-blade (plastic) or rubber-edged shovel, and shovel the snow before it partially melts and refreezes.

It has been revealed that “Avoid pushing your shovel into cracks or potholes, and don’t bang it against the surface in an attempt to dislodge stubborn ice,” indicates Lopez. “Instead, choose a deicing product that’s safe for asphalt.”.

It has been revealed that A shovel can easily catch the edge of a paver and scratch, break or knock it out of place. To prevent that, use a poly-blade shovel, take shorter shovel strokes, push snow at an angle and slightly raise up the leading edge.

In a recent development, “Shoveling and deicing aggressively won’t make your job faster or easier, it takes some finesse,” indicates Lopez. Also, use de-icers that are safe for both the paving and jointing material, and inspect the walkway for loose bricks once the snow melts.

After a snow, it can be tricky to tell where the concrete ends and the lawn begins, and one wrong move means damaged grass come springtime. To keep from marring your grass, mark walkway edges with small flags before it snows. While shoveling, keep the blade even with your walkway, versus angling it toward the grass.

Pro-tip: “Slow down and work in short passes near the edges, rather than trying to force the shovel along,” states Lopez. “.

In a recent development, try not to pile snow on shrubs and other perennials, as that can snap branches. It’s also best to keep deicers and their runoff away from landscaping.

“Before winter arrives, plan where you’ll pile or toss snow to keep it away from sensitive plants,” states Lopez. “You may find it helpful to use a smaller shovel, which will give you better control over where the snow lands.”.

Also, try not to move soil, which can expose plants to the cold, and never strike frozen branches to remove snow. “Wood breaks more easily than people expect,” says moving professional Leon Schwab.

Aggressive shoveling is sure to damage a deck, regardless of its composition. To preserve yours, use a poly-blade shovel and push the snow in the direction of the boards. If it’s safe to do so, leave a thin layer of snow, instead of shoveling all the way down to bare decking, then apply a deicer that’s recommended for the surface type.

Industry observers note that safety tip: “If wet, heavy snow is accumulating and you notice the deck sagging or hear creaking noises, seek professional advice,” says Lopez. “Don’t continue using the deck if you suspect a structural issue.”.

Stairs are particularly hazardous when its slippery out, and clearing them can be precarious, with snow obscuring their boundaries and confined spaces limiting your range of motion.

It has been revealed that to stay safe, “Wear boots with good traction and make sure your staircase is well lit,” states Lopez. “Don’t rush the job. It’s better to take your time and shovel safely.”.

Pro-tip: “Use a small shovel to clear one step at a time and maintain a stable position,” states Schwab.

Sometimes it’s prudent to clear large accumulations of snow from the roof, but it’s also a dangerous job. To stay safe, roofing contractor Andre Kazimierski recommends using a roof rake, which allows you to pull off snow while remaining on the ground. Focus on clearing off as much as you can, but don’t worry about leaving it completely bare, and try not to touch your roofing material.

It has been revealed that “Do this sooner rather than later, because if it starts to warm up a bit the snow will become denser and heavier, making it harder to remove,” says Kazimierski. “And never walk on your roof when it’s even the slightest bit snowy or icy up there.”.

Sources indicate that obviously, you don’t want to take a shovel to your car, as that would do a lot of damage. Instead, use a snow brush or broom that’s designed to be gentle on vehicle finishes. Flores recommends this one from Snow Joe.

According to recent reports, start by clearing the roof in sections, then move on to the hood, trunk, windows, headlights, taillights and mirrors. You’ll especially want to get the roof and hood fully clear; otherwise, once you start driving, snow can blow up or slide down onto your windshield, obstructing your vision and endangering other drivers. “That ice can fly off your car at 40 miles per hour,” says Flores.
