It has been revealed that homeowners with boxelder trees (a type of maple tree that produces seed-bearing pods) may be all too familiar with the bugs that tend to follow. Boxelder bugs, named for their preferred host, are ½-inch-long black insects with red or orange markings along their wings. They feed on seeds and leaves from boxelders and a few other trees like ash and maple, but they don’t cause serious damage to plants, homes, or humans. Still, when these bugs gather in large numbers, they become a major nuisance—especially when they invade homes and release their distinctive, musty smell.

Sources indicate that in fall, boxelder bugs migrate toward warmth, often swarming on the south- and west-facing walls of homes, garages, sheds, and trees. If they find small cracks or gaps, they’ll slip inside to overwinter in walls, attics, or basements—sometimes appearing indoors on sunny winter days. Even homes without box elder trees nearby aren’t entirely safe: These bugs are highly attracted to warmth and light-colored siding, making them a common seasonal pest in many regions.

If you’re tired of seeing these bugs on your siding—or worse, inside your house—take charge now with these smart strategies for getting rid of boxelder bugs.

Sources indicate that boxelder bugs (Boisea trivittata) are easy to recognize once you know what to look for. Adult bugs are about ½ inch long, with black bodies and reddish-orange markings along their wings and thorax. Their long, oval shape and bold color contrast make them easy to spot—especially when they gather in large groups on sunny walls or trees.

Juvenile boxelder bugs, known as nymphs, are smaller and bright red with no wings, though they develop darker coloration and wing pads as they mature. You’ll typically see these bugs in late summer and fall, when both adults and nymphs are most active.

Despite their intimidating appearance, boxelder bugs are harmless to people, pets, and homes. They don’t bite or sting, and they won’t eat through drywall, wood, or furniture. However, their tendency to swarm in large numbers—and release a pungent odor when crushed—makes them a frustrating nuisance pest, especially when they get indoors.

Industry observers note that boxelder bugs are often mistaken for other insects, like stink bugs or milkweed bugs. What sets them apart is their distinctive red-lined wings, flattened body, and preference for warm, sunlit surfaces. If you notice clusters of bugs on the south or west sides of your home, windows, or trees in fall, you’re likely dealing with boxelder bugs.

It has been revealed that boxelder bugs follow a predictable seasonal pattern, which explains why they seem to appear all at once. In spring, adults emerge from their overwintering spots—usually inside walls or attics—and head outdoors to feed and lay eggs on box elder, maple, and ash trees.

By summer, the eggs hatch into bright red nymphs, which mature into winged adults by late summer. These adults become most visible in fall, when they gather in large numbers on sunlit walls and tree trunks, especially on the south and west sides of homes.

As temperatures drop, they look for cracks and gaps in buildings to overwinter indoors. Though mostly dormant through winter, they may occasionally reappear on warm, sunny days—often near windows or light sources.

Knowing their seasonal behavior makes it easier to time prevention efforts, especially in early fall when they begin looking for a way inside.

If the bugs are in your house, don’t panic—they won’t bite, sting, or reproduce inside. Still, their smell and stains can be unpleasant. Use these simple methods to get them out and keep them from coming back.

Boxelder bugs slip in through small cracks around windows, doors, vents, and siding.

In a recent development, do this in early fall before they try to move in for winter. Once they’re inside, they’re much harder to control.

Boxelder bugs often hide in basements, attics, or ceiling corners, especially during colder months. To catch the sneaky ones, set up glue or light-based traps in these low-traffic areas.

Replace traps regularly to avoid lingering odors. While traps won’t eliminate a boxelder bug infestation, they’re a great supplemental tool for catching stragglers inside the home.

For quick, chemical-free control, just vacuum up any boxelder bugs you find on floors, windowsills, or walls.

Boxelder bugs don’t reproduce indoors. Once you’ve cleared them out and sealed up entry points, they shouldn’t come back.

Instead of reaching for harsh chemical pesticides (they’re not very helpful here), mix up a DIY soap spray to kill boxelder bugs on contact.

Boxelder bugs are most active outdoors in late summer and fall, especially around sunny walls, tree trunks, and light-colored siding. Taking action early can reduce the number trying to get indoors.

If you spot small groups of boxelder bugs gathering on your home’s siding, foundation, or trees, a strong blast from a garden hose can break them up.

Reducing their numbers outside can help you avoid a full-blown infestation indoors later on.

For larger swarms, diatomaceous earth is a natural and pet-safe way to kill boxelder bugs outdoors.

According to recent reports, this fine powder pierces the bugs’ exoskeletons, causing them to dry out and die within hours. Reapply diatomaceous earth after it rains, or if the bugs return.

It has been revealed that in general, chemical sprays are not the first recommendation for managing boxelder bugs. Experts at the University of California Integrated Pest Management program advise that insecticide sprays are often no more effective than vacuuming or using a garden hose, and require repeated application for limited results.

However, if bugs are clustered on the exterior of your house and you’ve already tried sealing, trapping, vacuuming, and all of these other recommendations, a professional-grade perimeter spray may help. For persistent infestations in late summer or early fall, a licensed pest professional may apply EPA-approved synthetic pyrethroid insecticides (like deltamethrin, bifenthrin, cyfluthrin, or permethrin) to the foundation, siding seams, eaves, window and door trim, and attic vents to create a residual barrier.

In a recent development, since the pests feed on the seedpods of female box elder trees, removing them and replacing them with non-seed-bearing male trees (or other species) can help you get rid of the bugs permanently. Keep in mind that the more mature the tree, the costlier it will be to remove. Also, consider that the benefits of the tree—shade, privacy, and curb appeal—may outweigh the insect nuisance.

Warm fall weather and nearby box elder, maple, or ash trees attract the bugs to sunlit walls and cracks.

Remove seed-bearing trees, seal entry points, clean up debris, and use non-chemical control methods.

Industry observers note that there’s no proven scent that reliably repels them, despite some anecdotal claims. You’re usually better off using a light trap or a hose to spray them away.

No—vinegar may deter them briefly, but it doesn’t kill them.

Yes, if DIY methods fail or infestations are large and persistent, call in the pros.

GTA6 let's you take a break from a life of crime to make some much-needed home repairs on Jason and Lucia's house.

Industry observers note that just in case your algorithm is different from mine, here’s some news: Grand Theft Auto 6 officially released today. After 13 years of waiting, fans of the open-world action-adventure video game series can finally dive into a newly introduced, richly detailed and fully realized virtual world. Boot up the game, and you’ll find yourself faced with surprising realism, a world of crime, and the ability to do just about whatever you want. That’s right, even… DIY home improvement jobs?

According to recent reports, yep, you’re reading that right. As part of its commitment to realism, GTA developer Rockstar Games has given players the ability to do some honest-to-goodness, roll-up-your-sleeves-and-get-to-work home improvement virtually.

And it’s not just a short cutscene where you see the house magically go from disrepair to fully fixed up. You, as the player, have to actually do the work, whether you’re drywalling, painting, or roofing. Luckily, it’s just a video game because the game is also set in a fictional version of Florida in the summer, which is probably one of the last places on earth you’d want to be stuck doing any sort of construction work.

Let’s take a look at a few of the home improvement jobs done by GTA6‘s Jason Duval and see if his work meets Family Handyman’s standards.

With his lady friend Lucia on the way back from prison, Jason decides to fix up the place… including the unfinished framing in the center of his living room. Luckily, Jason knows how to hang drywall. The gameplay represents the job pretty accurately— Jason holds the drywall in place and screws it into the studs with an impact driver. We don’t get to see any taping or mudding, though. 7/10.

Sources indicate that next, we’ll inspect whether Jason should perhaps prioritize a career as a painter over his life of crime. The painting section is also pretty accurate to the average DIY painting experience. Jason has to choose between three different color options before pouring the paint into a tray and using a roller to paint the wall. It’s pretty boring, which is honestly just like painting in real life — so bonus points for immersive realism. 8/10.

Recent findings suggest that one of the first things Jason knows he has to fix before Lucia arrives is the massive hole in his roof that’s letting in a near-constant drip of rain. Luckily, like a lot of DIYers, he has some roofing experience, a cordless nail gun and a stack of shingles just lying around for some reason. Again, this section is pretty realistic. If gamers want the full Florida roofing experience, though, they’ll have to crank their heaters to maximum or perhaps play the game in a sauna. 6/10.

Look, I get it. The Grand Theft Auto series is about living out fantasies, providing gamers a sandbox where they can virtually experience the impossible.

Industry observers note that but still… “House repairs complete” is a bridge too far. Ask any DIYer, and they will tell you no house is ever fully repaired. Pretending home improvement work could ever be finished is just not realistic and really took me out of the experience. 3/10.

Overall, the game is cool. But to be honest, I’m not sure what the point is now that the house repairs are complete.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, the motion arises from an altercation between respondent and participants in a demonstration outside of the federal courthouse for the Southern District of New York on September 29, 2025.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From a N.Y. appellate decision Thursday in Att'y Grievance Comm. v. Fernich (Judges Sallie Manzanet-Daniels, Tanya R. Kennedy, Barbara R. Kapnick, Kelly O'Neill Levy, and Matthew Parker-Raso); the respondent, Marc Fernich, is a prominent Fresh York criminal defense lawyer, who represented, among others, Jeffrey Epstein, John Gotti, and Joaquin Guzman (drug cartel leader El Chapo):.

According to recent reports, the motion arises from an altercation between respondent and participants in a demonstration outside of the federal courthouse for the Southern District of New York on September 29, 2025. On May 27, 2026, the AGC served respondent with a notice and petition of charges alleging one charge of professional misconduct under Rules of Professional Misconduct (22 NYCRR 1200.0) rule 8.4(h), which prohibits conduct that adversely reflects on the lawyer's fitness as a lawyer. The parties have submitted a stipulation of facts, respondent's affidavit, and materials addressing aggravation and mitigation. Respondent admits to the stipulated misconduct, acknowledges the consequences of consenting to discipline, and agrees to a public censure.

On September 29, 2025, respondent, then 61 years old, was leaving a meeting at the Newly introduced York County District Attorney's Office and was walking toward the Brooklyn Bridge. On Centre Street, he came upon a group of demonstrators in support of Palestine outside of the federal courthouse. Some demonstrators were singing and chanting, one played a guitar, and others held a banner reading "Jewish Artists for Palestine.".

Respondent attempted to make his way through a circle of demonstrators, and admits that physical contact occurred as he attempted to proceed. Respondent grabbed a demonstrator's arm, pushed and grabbed others while moving through the circle, and engaged in heated verbal confrontation. The cellphone recordings of the incident also show respondent holding a demonstrator from behind with his arms around the person's waist, with the demonstrator shouting at him to remove his arms, respondent pushing and grabbing others, and respondent holding another demonstrator from behind with his arms around the individual's neck.

Among other things, respondent's threatening and antisemitic remarks included "Back off me, Kapo, Kike, Jew Boy!," "You fucking animal, you're worse than a fucking Muslim!," "You should have been aborted," and "You should have been thrown into an oven, I'd throw you in if I could!" He also mentioned that the demonstrators' grandparents should have died in the Holocaust, as well as other inflammatory remarks invoking violence. Respondent remained at the demonstration for approximately one hour, until it ended.

It has been revealed that at his deposition, respondent maintained that the video depiction of the incident was a compilation of cellphone recordings made by several individuals and that they were out of sequence and out of context. He asserted that the confrontation had not been one-sided; demonstrators had been linking arms, blocking his way, pushing back, and squeezing his genitals.

In a recent development, he also maintained that the recordings had purposefully omitted much of the physical contact and extreme anti-Israel and anti-Zionist rhetoric directed at him. Nonetheless, he recognized that the demonstrators had been exercising their constitutional rights to assemble and engage in free speech, and that his words and actions could not be justified. He was deeply ashamed of his conduct and expressed remorse.

The parties have stipulated that respondent's misconduct is aggravated by his substantial experience in the practice of law. They have also stipulated to considerable mitigation. Respondent has no prior disciplinary history. The incident was unrelated to his representation of a client or the practice of law, and did not disrupt a court proceeding. Respondent self-reported his misconduct to the AGC through counsel, cooperated with the AGC investigation, voluntarily appeared for examination, accepted responsibility, and expressed remorse and embarrassment for his actions. Fifteen character references described respondent as being well-regarded in the community and having character traits of honesty, integrity, and trustworthiness.

The record further reflects that respondent was experiencing significant medical issues at the time of the incident. He was recovering from a recent back surgery and experiencing significant pain, and had undergone emergency surgery for retinal tears shortly beforehand. He was also undergoing psychiatric treatment and taking medication for depression, anxiety, and ADHD. A report submitted by respondent's treating psychiatrist explains how the pain, emotional distress, and psychiatric symptoms respondent was experiencing may have contributed to his impaired judgment and agitation and, while respondent had been under his care for 13 years, he would never have expected him to engage in the kind of "angry and out-of-control conduct that he engaged in outside the Courthouse." Respondent, who has family in Israel, also maintains that the October 7, 2023 attacks in Israel affected him deeply and that his memory of those attacks caused his anger to boil over.

Under 22 NYCRR 1240.8(a)(5), the Court may resolve a disciplinary matter by consent where the submissions establish an admitted violation and an appropriate agreed-upon sanction. In support of the proposal for a public censure, the parties cite decisions imposing a censure for similarly offensive, abusive, and discriminatory remarks and other isolated misconduct (see e.g. Matter of Melogy, 233 AD3d 135 [1st Dept 2024]; Matter of Mukambetova, 204 AD3d 158 [1st Dept 2022]; Matter of Schlossberg, 192 AD3d 8 [1st Dept 2020]).

Recent findings suggest that respondent's use of antisemitic and threatening language, together with his physical aggression towards demonstrators, warrants public discipline. At the same time, the absence of a disciplinary history, the isolated nature of the incident, the medical and psychological circumstances, his cooperation, and his acceptance of responsibility supports the sanction jointly proposed. Public censure appropriately expresses the profession's condemnation of the relevant conduct while also recognizing the substantial mitigation.

Accordingly, the parties' joint motion for discipline by consent pursuant to 22 NYCRR 1240.8(a)(5) should be granted, … and respondent publicly censured….

Jorge Dopico and Raymond Vallejo represent the Committee.

Thankfully, experts in the home decor space are sharing their seasonal tips to help you get ready.

HGTV’s Jonathan Scott shared a video with a few Christmas decorating hacks he and his partner, Zooey Deschanel, use in their home.

“I like it to be a little bit nostalgic, a little bit fun, and a whole lot of holiday spirit,” Scott says.

According to recent reports, there’s no one right way to decorate for Christmas, and even if so that doesn’t mean you should stick to the conventional script, according to Scott. “There are lots of different rules when decorating for the holidays, but of course, as we know, rules are meant to be broken,” Scott indicates. “So it really depends on your comfort level.”.

Here are some of Scott’s hacks:.

Sources indicate that even the nicest artificial trees can look a little too perfect. Scott’s trick is to stuff a few extra branches into the tree, leaving some sticking out at random. He also adds more lights, including larger bulbs, even though his tree is already pre-lit.

Scott has been collecting nutcrackers for years, and yes, he even names them. Rather than display them the same way every Christmas, he changes things up with different garlands, beads, and branches. It’s a way to get a new look out of decorations he already owns.

According to recent reports, those giant stacked presents in Scott’s house look like they’d be a pain to store, but they’re not. Each box fits inside the next, so the whole display takes up a fraction of the space once Christmas is over.

You can watch the full video and get more tips here:.

At the top of everyone’s mind around the holidays should be safety.

Scott recommends being mindful of fragile decorations, especially if you have young children or large pets. Glass ornaments and other breakable decorations can easily get knocked over, so consider using sturdier pieces in areas where kids and pets spend a lot of time.

Sources indicate that the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) also recommends looking for a “fire resistant” label when purchasing an artificial Christmas tree and regularly watering live trees to reduce fire risks.

Whether you’re adding a few fresh touches to your favorite decorations or going all out with a Christmas tree in every room, the most key thing is creating a space that feels festive to you.

#193193. Tech Report: Social Media Platforms Not Liable for Racist Buffalo Mass Shooting, Notes N.Y. High Court by 4-3 Vote

Tech Report: Social Media Platforms Not Liable for Racist Buffalo Mass Shooting, Notes N.Y. High Court by 4-3 Vote

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2926 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that from the 4-judge unsigned majority opinion in Patterson v.
  • On May 14, 2022, a man motivated by heinous white supremacist ideologies he allegedly adopted due to content he viewed on social media carried out a mass shooting at a Buffalo grocery store, killing 10 and injuring three others.
  • According to recent reports, these appeals concern motions to dismiss plaintiffs' claims against several social media companies whose platforms the shooter allegedly used before committing this unspeakable act of violence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that from the 4-judge unsigned majority opinion in Patterson v. Meta Platforms, Inc., decided today by N.Y.'s high court:.

On May 14, 2022, a man motivated by heinous white supremacist ideologies he allegedly adopted due to content he viewed on social media carried out a mass shooting at a Buffalo grocery store, killing 10 and injuring three others. Plaintiffs, victims of the shooting and their family members, commenced these actions against the shooter's parents, firearms manufacturers, and social media companies, seeking compensation for their injuries.

According to recent reports, these appeals concern motions to dismiss plaintiffs' claims against several social media companies whose platforms the shooter allegedly used before committing this unspeakable act of violence. Specifically, plaintiffs contend that their complaints state causes of action for products liability based on defective features of these social media defendants' platforms and their failure to warn thereof….

[P]laintiffs failed to adequately plead that features of [the] social media defendants' products proximately caused their injuries. Generally, a defendant's acts qualify as a proximate cause when they are "a substantial cause of the events which produced the injury." This inquiry examines.

"the foreseeability of the event resulting in injury; the passage of time between the originally negligent act and the intervening act; the spatial gap, if any, between the original act and the intervening act; whether the original act of negligence was a completed occurrence or was ongoing at the time of the intervening act; whether and, if so, what other forces combined to bring about the harm; as well as public policy considerations regarding the scope of liability.".

Foreseeability is often the most significant factor. Indeed, if an unforeseeable intervening criminal act of a third party causes the plaintiff's injury, the causal connection is severed. Thus, proximate causation will not be found when the intervening act "is extraordinary under the circumstances, not foreseeable in the normal course of events, or independent of or far removed from the defendant's conduct." "Although foreseeability and proximate cause are generally questions for the factfinder, there are instances in which proximate cause can be determined as a matter of law because 'only one conclusion may be drawn from the established facts'" such as when "the original negligent act merely 'furnished the occasion for'—but did not cause—'an unrelated act to cause injuries not ordinarily anticipated.'".

According to recent reports, here, plaintiffs failed to adequately allege that the remaining social media defendants' product defects proximately caused the shooter to carry out the mass shooting that resulted in plaintiffs' injuries. The complaints, even accepting the factual allegations as true, fail to establish that the shooter's actions were a natural and foreseeable consequence of these defendants' decisions about how to design and operate their platforms.

Instead, under the circumstances, the shooter's actions were so extraordinary as to sever the causal chain as a matter of law. {Our conclusion is limited to the unusual facts of this case, where the platforms' assertedly addictive features were alleged to have harmed the shooter rather than the plaintiffs directly.} We therefore need not address the scope of section 230 of the Communications Decency Act or how it would apply to the claims against these defendants.

Judge Halligan joined the majority, but also wrote a concurring opinion:.

I join the majority because I agree that the plaintiffs have not adequately pleaded proximate causation. I write separately to underscore that, for me, this conclusion rests squarely on the highly unusual facts presented here, and to offer some additional thoughts regarding the scope of section 230.

As an initial matter, I agree with my dissenting colleagues that the plaintiffs alleged that several of the defendants tortiously designed addictive products. The complaints make a number of general claims about social media and youth: that defendants' platforms are addictive; that compulsive use of social media, particularly by young people, causes emotional disturbance and "impulsive decision-making and risk-taking behavior"; and that such use can also yield other deleterious consequences, including "sleep disturbances, mental health problems and suicidal ideation, and violent, hateful acts." The complaints further assert that the social media defendants, knowing of the addictive quality of their products and the heightened susceptibility of young customers, not only failed to implement features for limiting use or warning parents, but also took deliberate advantage of that vulnerability by utilizing "strategic timing and clustering of notifications to lure back users" and by implementing "barriers to the deactivation and deletion of accounts." ….

I find the claims before us quite distinct from the cases cited by the dissent that have allowed products liability claims premised on the addictiveness of social media platforms to proceed. I have little doubt that a plaintiff could allege a sufficient connection between the design of a platform and adverse consequences for the mental health of young customers. In those cases, the harms that form the basis for the claims—for example, the alleged inducement of "compulsive use among young users to the detriment of their health and well-being"—flow directly from the platforms' allegedly defective features, leaving little question "that the defective design was a substantial factor in causing plaintiff's injury.".

Recent findings suggest that but the plaintiffs here are not bringing a claim on behalf of users. Instead, they are seeking recompense for the victims of a crime committed by a social media user. In other words, the allegedly addictive properties of the platforms were not alleged to have harmed the plaintiffs here directly, but rather to have harmed the shooter, who in turn engaged in extensive research and planning before murdering ten people and wounding others…. I do not see the connection between the two as sufficiently articulated to allow the case to proceed.

According to recent reports, three aspects of these claims inform my conclusion. First, although intervening criminal acts do not necessarily sever the causal chain, the shooter's conduct was apparently painstakingly planned and extraordinarily violent.

Second, the prominence of content in many of plaintiffs' allegations gives me real pause. Even if we were to interpret section 230 as not immunizing defendants against claims for actions that rest, at least in part, on content, I am not aware of other instances where a court has held that provocative content proximately caused someone to commit a violent crime, and I am hesitant to take that step here. {I understand the plaintiffs to disclaim on appeal any effort to base liability on defendants' roles as publishers of content. But their complaints can be read to allege that the platforms are defective at least in part because of the racist and extremist content they make available, and the plaintiffs acknowledge that content is a necessary link in the causal chain leading to their harms.}.

In a recent development, third, the defendants' platforms have billions of worldwide users. To the extent that proximate cause could rest on a correlation between social media use and a specific type of harmful act committed by any one of those users, the potential liability would sweep broadly, to say the least. If all such conduct were "a natural and foreseeable consequence" of a platform's design choices, the concept of proximate cause would have little meaning….

As for section 230, …. "we [have] read section 230 to bar 'lawsuits seeking to hold a service provider liable for its exercise of a publisher's traditional editorial functions.'" … Our endorsement of a "traditional editorial functions" test for section 230 immunity, however, does little to answer whether the conduct of modern social media platforms can be labelled such a function.

It has been revealed that as to claims that a defendant designed its platform features to encourage or facilitate addiction, irrespective of the particular content promoted by the platform, I agree with the dissent that they are not barred by section 230. That is because such conduct does not constitute a traditional editorial function, even under a broad understanding of that term.

As to claims that challenge a social media platform's use of content-recommendation algorithms, the dissent appears to take the view that content-recommendation algorithms which are designed to be addictive are not covered by section 230 immunity, since they increase engagement in a way that could not have been envisioned at the time that provision was enacted in 1996. I have no quarrel with how we framed the scope of section 230 in Shiamili: the key question is whether a platform engaged in a traditional editorial function, akin to a decision "to publish, withdraw, postpone or alter content." But whether platforms' use of content-recommendation algorithms can be mentioned to resemble traditional decisions to publish, withdraw, postpone, or alter content is, for me, a more difficult question….

[O]verly broad interpretations of section 230 in the face of a rapidly changing technological landscape are unmoored from Congress's purpose in enacting that provision—to protect minors from being exposed to pornography online…. Given that caution, I would not be inclined to extend section 230's reach to all content-recommendation algorithms. I am particularly skeptical that use of individualized content-recommendation algorithms—that is, algorithms that "assess[ ] a user's prior posts, friends, or viewing habits to recommend latest content and connections"—constitutes a traditional publisher function. After all, "[t]raditional publication has never included selecting the news, opinion pieces, or classified ads to send to each individual reader based on guesses as to their preferences and interests." Instead, such functions may be "more analogous to the actions of a direct marketer, matchmaker, or recruiter than to those of a publisher.".

In my view, a closer question is presented as to engagement-maximizing algorithms that, unlike the algorithms described above, do not take into account any individual user's conduct but instead seek to "promote[ ] third-party content" based on "cumulative user engagement." On one hand, algorithms that do not respond to individual user conduct may be thought to resemble a publisher's traditional aim of presenting content that owners, on the whole, want to see. On the other hand, one might conclude that "generic" content-based algorithms bear no more resemblance to traditional publication than their "'advanced'—individualized—counterparts" because they still rely on an assessment of user viewing habits in a manner akin to "a direct marketer" rather than a traditional publisher. My dissenting colleagues offer yet another variation on this point; they assert that engagement-maximizing algorithms differ from an editor's choice of where to place a news story because the algorithms are "designed to prey on neurological frailties and alter brain chemistry.".

Recent findings suggest that whether section 230 protects any of these algorithms is, for me, a difficult question, and I do not think the record before us sheds much light on how different types of content-recommendation algorithms actually operate on the social media defendants' individual platforms—information that might affect my view. We need not decide those questions today because, whatever the scope of the "traditional editorial functions" protected by section 230, the plaintiffs have failed to sufficiently allege that the defendants' platforms' features caused their grave injuries.

Judge Rivera, joined by Chief Judge Wilson and Judge Troutman, dissented in relevant part; an excerpt from the very long opinion:.

It has been revealed that the complaints detail the shooter's transformation from a seemingly ordinary teenager into a virulent racist and violent white supremacist…. [In his manifesto, t]he shooter also wrote that he "was not born racist nor [did he] gr[o]w up to be racist." Rather, he was exposed to and indoctrinated in his ideology of racial violence after using various social media platforms, starting with Instagram, YouTube, and Snapchat in his early teen years, before he transitioned to more niche platforms like Reddit, Discord, Twitch and 4chan. The shooter claimed he swiftly "became transfixed with and addicted to [the] online world." He wrote in his diary:.

In a recent development, "I'm addict[ed] to consoooooming. It's 2 in the morning. w[hat] t[he] f[*ck] … I'll admit my mental health has seriously degraded these past few years, especially in the last few months. I should be sleeping right now. I'm just browsing online:/" (emphasis added).

By his own account, he sacrificed "years of [his] life" to being online, often "stay[ing] up late" "browsing Reddit or watching YouTube" "every day." He stated that his compulsive social media use "seriously degraded" his mental health and isolated him from his peers. Rather than "go[ing] to friend's houses" or other social gatherings, "[e]very day after school [he] would just go home and play games and watch YouTube, mostly by [him]self." Ultimately, as he descended further into isolation, he believed he had no other choice but to commit this barbarous act.

Sources indicate that plaintiffs allege that the shooter's experience of compulsive social media engagement is widespread because the products' addictive features are fundamental to the social media defendants' business model. According to plaintiffs, defendants' business models seek to maximize user engagement through products "designed to be addictive." Plaintiffs assert that the operation of these products on the shooter, and their adverse impact on his mind caused by their addictive features, are links in the proximate causal chain underlying plaintiffs' tort liability causes of action against the social media defendants….

In a recent development, the Appellate Division erroneously concluded that defendants are immune from plaintiffs' lawsuit under Section 230. As I discuss, Section 230 does not shield defendants from plaintiffs' products liability and failure to warn allegations grounded on allegedly addictive products, as those claims have nothing to do with defendants' role as a third-party content publisher or as the creator of protected speech….

Sources indicate that to the extent plaintiffs' claims against the social media defendants are based upon defendants' publication of third-party content, including racist, white supremacist, and violent content, defendants are immune from suit pursuant to Section 230. However, not all claims asserted in the complaints are based upon defendants' publication of third-party content. Rather, as I explain, the complaints also stated causes of action based on defendants' design of allegedly defective products and failure to warn….

In a recent development, plaintiffs assert that these defendants are civilly liable for their role in addicting the shooter to social media and consequent deterioration of his mental health. Plaintiffs' complaints set forth the entire chain of causation that allegedly led to the mass shooting. By designing highly addictive algorithms known to cause severe mental harm to teenagers—like the shooter—the social media defendants created a direct link to the resulting damages, particularly given their failure to warn consumers and parents of these risks…. [T]here is no Section 230 immunity that attaches to the architecture of defendants' social media products—particularly their purposefully addictive algorithms….

Defendants' alternative argument that the complaints were properly dismissed on First Amendment grounds is unpersuasive. At this pre-answer stage of the litigation, it is unclear how precisely the content-recommendation algorithms function, meaning it is not possible to determine, as a matter of law, on a motion to dismiss that the algorithms themselves are protected speech. That determination requires factual findings dependent on future discovery. On a motion to dismiss we only decide whether the plaintiffs' claim is cognizable and not whether it will eventually succeed based on the facts established by the record….

And here's a short excerpt from the dissent's long discussion of why it rejects the majority's proximate cause theory:.

Sources indicate that the majority's conclusion that plaintiffs "fail to establish that the shooter's actions were a natural and foreseeable consequence" of the social media defendants' platforms because "the shooter's actions were so extraordinary as to sever the causal chain as a matter of law" is unsupported by our well-established tort liability doctrines. First, we have made clear that there may be more than one link in a causal chain and there may be more than one tortfeasor liable, jointly or individually, for a plaintiff's injuries. "[T]he mere fact that other persons share some responsibility for [the] plaintiff's harm does not absolve [a] defendant from liability." Thus, the fact that the third-party content creators may bear responsibility for the harm does not mean that defendants bear none.

Second, a defect need only be a "substantial cause"—not the sole cause—"of the events which produced the injury." Substantial means more than slight or trivial. Plaintiffs' allegations that defendants' product adversely affected the shooter's mental health and behavior, making him a compulsive social media user, with the attendant negative impact on his mind and body, isolated from others, rendering him more susceptible to commit this horrific violent act, easily satisfies the "substantial cause" standard.

Industry observers note that third, not all intervening acts break the causal chain. An intervening act only breaks the causal nexus if it is extraordinary under the circumstances, unforeseeable in the normal course of events, or independent of and far removed from the defendant's conduct. That determination depends on whether the intervening act and its consequences were the foreseeable result of a defendant's tortious conduct. Even the "intentional" or "criminal" intervening acts of a third party can be reasonably foreseeable….

It has been revealed that [W]hile here, the harm arose from exposure to graphic violence and white supremacist propaganda, plaintiffs allege that the algorithm is content-agnostic. According to plaintiffs, defendants' products and platforms rely on these complex algorithms to keep users engaged, which negatively impacts young people's mental health, and, in turn, increases the tendency to violent behavior, all the while driving revenue for these defendants. Thus, the majority's assertion that the shooter's actions were not foreseeable is nothing more than a factual conclusion, but that determination cannot be made by the Court on a motion to dismiss….

Recent findings suggest that the best countertop water filtration system for your home will depend on the quality concerns you want to address, how much filtered water your household uses, and how much daily upkeep you’re willing to take on. It’s smart to request a copy of your local utility’s Consumer Confidence Report or use a home water test kit, then compare potential systems’ filtration claims, capacity, footprint, and replacement-filter cost.

Countertop water filters generally fall into two broad categories: reservoir-based systems and faucet-connected systems. Reservoir models don’t connect to your plumbing at all, while faucet-connected models attach to a standard faucet or use a diverter valve under your sink.

Reservoir systems hold untreated water in one tank or chamber and deliver clean water into another after it passes through the system’s filter(s). The simplest versions are water pitchers like the Epic Water Filters Pure XP Water Filter Pitcher or gravity systems like the Big Berkey Gravity-Fed Water Filter. Since they don’t connect to your faucet, they’re great for apartments, dorms, RVs, and kitchens with incompatible faucets.

Countertop reverse osmosis systems also use a refillable reservoir, but rather than relying on gravity, they have an internal pump that forces the water through their filters before delivering it to a pitcher or your glass. RO systems have the added benefit of reducing dissolved solids in untreated water, but that includes beneficial minerals like calcium and magnesium and also creates wastewater that must be dumped (or used for things like cleaning or watering plants).

Faucet-connected filters either attach directly to your faucet or connect via a hose and diverter valve. When the diverter is switched to the filtration setting, tap water filters through the unit on demand and into your glass, bottle, or pot. When the diverter is off, water flows straight out of the tap as normal.

In a recent development, two major things to consider regarding faucet-connected systems are faucet compatibility and installation. Most aren’t compatible with pull-down, pull-out, spray, sensor-operated, or nonstandard faucets, and many also have small hoses that connect the faucet to the machine, which takes up a bit of space and can look cluttered. Some allow you to run the hoses from the machine to the plumbing under your sink, but that will require an adapter and a hole in the counter for the cords to route through.

While it can be tempting to choose the purification system for water that has the longest list of contaminants removed, it’s ultimately more vital to pair the system you choose with what you’re actually trying to filter out of your water.

Most of the best water filters have activated-carbon filters that remove unpleasant tastes and odors and may reduce other chemicals or particulates. Some systems add sediment filtration or specialty media to target things like lead, fluoride, or PFAS compounds. Since performance varies by model, always check the manufacturer’s claims rather than assuming they all work the same.

Sources indicate that reverse-osmosis systems use a membrane designed to reduce dissolved solids, which means they generally remove more contaminants than basic filtration systems. However, they can also reduce beneficial minerals, which is why some manufacturers are now adding a remineralization stage to return the filtered water to a more alkaline state.

It has been revealed that many of the units on this list carry third-party certification to verify tested performance beyond manufacturer claims. NSF International’s drinking-water treatment standards are the most commonly used, although you may also see mentions of accredited organizations like IAPMO R&T or WQA. While our tests using the Varify Complete Drinking Water Test Kit for this guide backed up the manufacturers’ claims, it’s still a good idea to prioritize products that carry filter certifications and look up which contaminants the product is certified to remove.

Sources indicate that then, match the certification to your specific concern. For example, if lead reduction is your main goal, you’ll want a model with NSF 53 and 58 listings.

Capacity has two meanings: how much water a filter can treat before replacement and how much filtered water the unit can provide at once. For our purposes, we’re defining it as how much it can filter at once, as we discuss filter life in the next section.

It has been revealed that since reservoir models’ ready-to-drink supply is based on the size of their clean-water chambers, larger households or those with greater needs will want to prioritize a model that holds multiple liters or gallons. Faucet-connected models can also be a good choice in those situations, as they can deliver clean water continuously as long as the tap is on.

Flow rate—how quickly the filter provides clean drinking water—is another key consideration. However, many manufacturers don’t list this information, and it can also vary depending on water pressure, source-water quality, temperature, and cartridge age. If this is a major concern, you may want to reach out to manufacturers directly or read online reviews for mentions of filtration speed.

Every countertop drinking water filter system requires filter replacement on a set schedule, which means the true cost of ownership ends up being more than what you paid for it. When choosing between systems, compare the number of filters, their individual projected filter capacity, and each one’s replacement cost.

Sources indicate that A basic pitcher may use a single cartridge that’s easy to change but needs more frequent replacement, while a multistage RO unit may have multiple filters that each have different change intervals and prices. While systems with filter-life indicators can make it much easier to know when it’s time to swap them, if your unit is noticeably slower or isn’t providing the same quality, you may still need to change filters even if it isn’t technically time.

Countertop water filters are generally pretty straightforward, but the following answers to commonly asked questions can answer any lingering queries you may have.

Water filters work by using a filtration mechanism to capture organisms and chemicals that lead to unsafe or cloudy water. A fabricated surface traps the larger contaminants, while a compound like activated carbon works as a magnet to trap smaller contaminants.

Installation depends on the type: A faucet-connected filtration system typically attaches to a compatible faucet aerator or diverter valve, while dispenser, pitcher, gravity-fed, and countertop RO models generally only require rinsing the parts, installing the filters, and filling the reservoir. Always follow the manufacturer’s instructions, especially for RO units that may also require an initial flush cycle.

No, countertop water purification filters do not work with every type of kitchen faucet. Specifically, more modern designs and detachable faucets with spray nozzles may be incompatible with faucet-connected countertop water filters.

Industry observers note that most filters can remove chlorine, fluoride, bacteria, and parasites. To know exactly which contaminants a specific filter can remove or reduce, consult the manufacturer’s information regarding filter certification.

Yes, bacteria can grow in a countertop filter, so it’s a good idea to flush the faucet for about 20 seconds after turning on the water and then for an additional 5 to 10 seconds to filter and flush out any bacteria that may be lingering in the faucet.

According to recent reports, yes, countertop reverse osmosis systems are worth it for households seeking to remove dissolved contaminants like lead and fluoride and who prefer a plumbing-free setup. However, they generally cost more and require more maintenance than pitchers or carbon-filter-only units, so they’re best when your water test or local report identifies concerns simpler filters can’t address.

In a recent development, filter replacement timing varies by system and filter type, so it’s best to follow the manufacturer’s schedule for your specific system. Generally speaking, pitcher and faucet units may need latest filters every few months, while countertop RO filters and membranes may last anywhere from 6 months to 2 years. You may need to replace filters sooner if the flow slows noticeably or your water develops an unusual taste or odor.

A thermal imaging camera detects infrared radiation emitted by objects and turns this into a visual representation of surface temperatures. Warmer (red, orange) and cooler (blue, purple) areas appear in contrasting colors, allowing you to see temperature differences that you can’t see with your own eyes.

This opens up some useful possibilities for homeowners. Imagine scanning around a window and spotting a cooler section along the frame. That doesn’t automatically mean there’s an air leak, but it’s a good reason to check the weatherstripping, caulking or surrounding insulation.

Wall Street delivered its verdict on the blue-wave midterms 48 hours later in the form of a red wave—red ink, that is.

Industry observers note that after a brief relief rally the day after the election, the Dow shed more than 1,800 points, the tech-heavy Nasdaq fell more than 5% and into correction territory, and roughly $2.5 trillion in market value vanished in a single session. Nvidia alone dropped more than 8%.

Recent findings suggest that market participants watched the collapse of the AI trade in real time—the bet that a massive buildout of data centers, chips, and software would power faster growth, higher productivity and rising wages for years to come. That theory hit the brick wall of an incoming Congress that has AI and data centers on their blacklist.

Sources indicate that democrats, who will comfortably control the Senate and hold their largest House majority in nearly two decades, have been far more hostile to data centers and AI than Republicans have. Several of their biggest wins came in places such as Texas, where local opposition to latest data centers had been building.

In a recent development, investors can read the writing on the wall: more regulation and taxation, slower permitting, and lower profits for AI and AI-adjacent companies. Since equity prices are ultimately justified by future earnings, adjusting those future expectations down also drove down equity prices.

>>> What’s Really Behind the Call to Regulate AI.

The fallout goes well beyond Silicon Valley. AI investment has been a key component of recent growth, and tens of millions of ordinary Americans own these companies through their 401(k)s. A slower buildout means fewer construction jobs, less demand for electricians and engineers, and slower productivity gains that drive real wage growth.

Recent findings suggest that the fiscal picture is dimmer, too. With Democrats running both chambers, there is no chance of further tax reform or meaningful spending cuts for at least two years. If a Republican Congress couldn't bring itself to enshrine the DOGE savings into law, a Democratic one certainly won't.

Instead, Democrat leaders are already promising to restore cost-increasing Obamacare subsidies and unwind recently implemented work-requirement reforms for welfare, all of which will layer new commitments on top of deficits already running at levels once seen only in wartime or recession.

Aside from burdening future generations with debt, these perpetual deficits have consequences for Americans today. The government is crowding out borrowing in the private sector, competing with families and businesses for loanable funds, thereby driving up interest rates on everything from mortgages to student loans to credit cards.

In a recent development, those higher borrower costs fall especially hard on those Americans that are already in debt and behind financially. The flood of government debt issuance also puts pressure on the Federal Reserve to help finance the debt by creating money to pay for perpetual deficits—a recipe for more inflation.

>>> Slowing Data Center Construction Signals the Need for Pro-Growth Reforms.

Unfortunately, a Democratic Congress will also likely offer no help on permitting reform, which is badly needed to build the pipelines, transmission lines and reliable power plants a growing economy requires.

Sources indicate that so the outlook is clearly worse, but why isn’t it terrible? Much of the consequential economic public policy changes of the past two years didn't depend on Congress, and it won’t go forward either. And while the tax-reform legislation passed last year obviously did require Congress, most of its provisions are permanent and won’t need reauthorization.

In a recent development, the administration retains broad authority to issue executive orders and roll back burdensome regulations. Cutting that red tape, on everything from energy production to banking, reduces compliance costs for Americans without a single vote on Capitol Hill.

Democrats will certainly try to slow that good work. Their leaders are already planning a wave of made-for-cable show trials that will drain time and attention from officials who should be dismantling the bureaucracy. But investigations can only delay regulatory reform, not stop it.

The president’s veto is another silver lining that will likely prevent the Democratic Congress from enacting sweeping tax hikes or newly introduced regulatory regimes. The worst ideas will hopefully die in committee or an Oval Office waste basket.

The economy has weathered worse than a hostile Congress. Ongoing deregulation and existing tax reform are still tailwinds for economic growth while the veto pen is there to stop headwinds as they arise. The outlook might be blue, but it’s not black and blue.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that the holidays are a great time to put up decorations around the home, either purchased decor or DIY options.
  • A recent viral video on a homeowner’s roof made it look like Santa is climbing into the chimney.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

A homemade Santa chimney display uses cardboard and pool noodles, but a roofing expert warns that this holiday craft could put a home at risk.

Recent findings suggest that the holidays are a great time to put up decorations around the home, either purchased decor or DIY options. Social feeds are full of ideas, but are all of them good or safe?

A recent viral video on a homeowner’s roof made it look like Santa is climbing into the chimney. It’s a creative chimney hack that might appeal to homeowners decorating for Christmas. But placing cardboard and other craft materials on a roof raises some safety concerns, especially during winter.

Learn what a roofing expert notes about the potential fire hazards, moisture problems, and safer alternatives.

A post shared by Drew (@thedrewsocial).

Not according to Andre Kazimierski, co-owner and president of HomeHero Roofing, a residential roofing company in Illinois.

“That decoration is definitely not wise to be putting up on your roof,” Kazimierski states. “Not only is it a fire hazard, but it’s likely going to create challenges with moisture.”.

According to recent reports, the cardboard and foam used in the decoration can catch fire, especially if they’re close to a working chimney. “Cardboard is flammable, so if it manages to catch on fire, it can then easily spread that fire to your roof,” Kazimierski warns.

According to recent reports, chimneys release heat and sometimes sparks, which could ignite nearby decorations. There’s also a risk of cardboard or other materials blocking the chimney opening, allowing smoke or dangerous gases to enter the home. Even if the fireplace isn’t in use, the chimney could still vent another heating appliance.

Rain and snow present another problem. “Cardboard can absorb a lot of water and get really soggy,” Kazimierski says.

Industry observers note that wet cardboard can collapse against the roof, while the paper covering and other decorations may start falling apart. Kazimierski warns that trapped moisture could also lead to mold, damaged roofing materials, or unwanted pests.

Industry observers note that moisture is already a concern for brick chimneys. “Common brick is like a sponge, absorbing water and wicking moisture to the chimney interior,” according to the Chimney Safety Institute of America. “Defective mortar joints or the use of improper mortar or brick can greatly increase the tendency to absorb and convey water to the interior of the masonry chimney structure.”.

A wet cardboard display resting against the chimney could keep the surrounding area damp, adding to existing moisture concerns.

Sources indicate that homeowners who want to decorate their roofs for Christmas should be careful about how they attach decorations. Nails and screws can puncture shingles, allowing water to seep underneath and potentially cause leaks.

It has been revealed that roofing manufacturer GAF recommends avoiding nails or staples when installing holiday decorations. Large displays can also damage shingles or come loose in strong winds.

Climbing onto the roof to install or remove decorations carries its own risks, particularly when the shingles are wet or covered in snow or ice.

According to recent reports, for homeowners who want to recreate the Santa chimney decoration, a safer option is to build a freestanding display on the porch or in the yard, away from the home’s actual chimney. Weather-resistant materials will hold up better than cardboard, and a sturdy base can help keep everything in place during windy weather.

If the display includes lights, the National Fire Protection Association recommends using decorations rated for outdoor use and checking electrical cords for damage.

Keeping the decoration at ground level also makes it easier to inspect, maintain, and remove without climbing onto the roof.

Last December, President Donald Trump introduced his vision for the United States Navy: a 30-year shipbuilding proposal called the “Golden Fleet.” Flanking him during his unveiling of this plan were renderings of a core component of that future Navy: USS Defiant, the lead ship of a new, modern class of battleship. But delivering it faces significant hurdles. The first is realistically addressing the Navy’s shaky shipbuilding track record. The second is surviving the changed political reality in Washington—made more challenging by Trump’s original plan to name the class of warship after himself.

By any name, the battleship addresses critical needs for the U.S. Navy. A modern battleship’s firepower, command and control, and data-fusion capabilities have been proven vital in recent conflicts in the Black Sea, the Red Sea, and the Persian Gulf. Mitigating shipbuilding risks, such as constrained production capacity and the integration of numerous advanced technologies, necessitate a continuous testing regimen that scales up as the ships are built.

The U.S. Navy Could Use a Modern “Battlecruiser” Warship.

The unveiling of the battleship comes as the Navy faces the imminent loss of significant at-sea firepower. By 2031, the departures of various submarines, cruisers, and destroyers will see nearly 2,000 missile-launch tubes lost. To blunt this loss, the next iteration of Virginia-class nuclear submarines will carry 28 hypersonic missiles, and the Navy’s unmanned vessels may also begin to carry offensive weapons.

Recent findings suggest that >>> The U.S. Navy Must Build the “Golden Fleet”.

The Navy missed an opportunity to address this firepower dilemma with its aborted CG(X) next-generation cruiser program, abandoned in 2011. These forced aging destroyers and Ticonderoga-class cruisers to continue shouldering the air and missile defense responsibilities for carrier strike groups. Flight III Arleigh Burke-class destroyers, however, lack the firepower and crew to fully assume the cruiser mission. The Arleigh Burke-class has 96 missile tubes, against 122 on the Ticonderoga-class, and has limited berthing for the needed staff to manage air and missile defenses for the carrier strike group.

In the long term, the Defiant and subsequent battleships are intended to fill this mission and firepower gap. The Defiant, with its added firepower, sensors and crew, will take over the Ticonderoga-class warships’ responsibilities for defending carrier strike groups. The ship will also employ long-range hypersonic missiles in support of carrier air-strike operations to rapidly suppress emerging threats.

The combination of capabilities merged in Defiant with sustained high speeds makes the vessel more closely resemble a battlecruiser—a high-speed battleship able to deliver long-range firepower and defend the carrier strike group from air and missile threats. However, recent battle lessons are creating another critical mission.

It has been revealed that the damage inflicted upon U.S. Fifth Fleet Headquarters in Bahrain, and its temporary evacuation due to Iranian missile debuts, demonstrates the vulnerability of permanent land-based naval installations to air attack. Moving headquarters to sea is one way to mitigate this danger, and follows a long tradition of numbered fleet command ships. A battlecruiser with robust command and control capabilities can maintain a common operational picture with the warships and unmanned platforms of its numbered fleet, reducing the Navy’s reliance on global communications.

>>> To Build the Golden Fleet.

How the Defiant Can Clear the Political Minefield on Capitol Hill.

According to recent reports, while battlecruisers are needed now, the United States faces numerous constraints that must be navigated before they can join the Golden Fleet. The high build cost of these ships will likely stir substantial resistance from budget-conscious members of Congress; a bill estimated by the Congressional Budget Office to be upwards of $23 billion for the first and subsequent ships costing $18 billion each. There are also serious shortages of skilled workers capable of efficiently building such intricate and substantial ships. Moreover, establishing upcoming or expanding existing shipyards to build these battlecruisers requires working through onerous shipbuilding regulations.

Keeping Congress’ support will necessitate reducing the potential for cost overruns and program delays. One way to accomplish this is to use proven technologies and systems in the initial design. Doing this would result in Defiant embracing existing systems to meet its mission requirements the soonest. Integrating systems like the hypersonic missile technologies being developed for the Zumwalt-class destroyers and the new AN/SPY-6 radars being installed in Arleigh Burke-class vessels will further compress production timelines.

In time, the design will need to be improved on through continuous updates—one being the transition to nuclear power to sustain high speeds and pace the aircraft carrier the battlecruiser is intended to protect. One option is using the same A1B nuclear power plant now used in the Ford-class aircraft carriers, given enough time for production to ramp up to support aircraft carrier and battlecruiser production.

Sources indicate that resurrecting the battlecruiser for modern naval missions is a highly ambitious initiative, and it may yet fall through. But it is needed to equip the U.S. Navy with the capabilities for fighting a modern naval war across the Pacific.

This piece originally appeared in The National Interest.

Sources indicate that my forthcoming chapter on "Emergency Powers" is now available on SSRN. It is coauthored with Josh Braver (University of Wisconsin), and will be published in the forthcoming Cato Handbook on Executive Power, edited by Molly Nixon. Braver is a leading expert on the law of domestic use of the military and a liberal/progressive. I am a a libertarian. If we can come to agreement on these issues, I hope others can, as well. Here is the abstract:.

Emergency powers are special types of government authorities that are only supposed to be used under extraordinary circumstances, in order to address a crisis. But, over time, many have become institutionalized as near-blank checks that the executive can invoke at will. This situation imperils civil liberties and our constitutional system.

This chapter goes over the major US emergency powers, including the National Emergencies Act, the Insurrection Act, the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), and others, and offers proposals for curbing the dangers they create. Effective reform requires a combination of new legislation and strong, nondeferential judicial review.

I recently covered related issues in an article for Just Security, which goes over potential legislative reforms. In the Cato Handbook chapter, Braver and I cover both legislative reforms and how judicial review can be strengthened.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve tested a lot of air purifiers, and most look like appliances I’d rather tuck out of sight in a corner. The Dupray Bloom Air Purifier is different. It combines a HEPA air purifier with a removable planter, turning something purely functional into a decorative accent. I planted a small fiddle-leaf fig in mine, and I love how it looks in the room. But I also wanted to know whether the Bloom’s unusual design would interfere with its primary job of filtering the air.

Recent findings suggest that absolutely, and that’s what makes the Bloom so appealing. The top features a removable planting pot with a root tray that helps keep roots above excess water. I chose a small fiddle-leaf fig, and once it was planted, the Bloom looked more like a decorative planter than an air-cleaning appliance.

There is one thing I’d caution buyers about: The planter doesn’t have drainage holes. The root tray provides some separation from standing water, but it isn’t a substitute for proper watering. I’d recommend using an olla, a small porous automatic watering vessel that slowly releases moisture into the soil. It’s a good option for keeping the plant watered without repeatedly pouring water into a pot that can’t drain.

In a recent development, I also appreciated that the planter lifts completely out. That means I can move the plant for maintenance or repotting without having to move the entire purifier. And when it’s time to replace the round HEPA filter, I can remove the planter, turn the unit over, and access the filter from the bottom.

Behind its decorative design, the Bloom is a serious air purifier. It uses an H13 HEPA filter with activated carbon to capture airborne particles, including dust, pollen, and pet dander, while helping reduce odors. Dupray rates it as capable of capturing 99.97 percent of particles as small as 0.1 micron.

It has been revealed that one feature I particularly liked was the stretchy fabric prefilter. It slips snugly over the purifier’s base, creating a smooth, modern appearance while catching larger airborne particles before they reach the HEPA filter. It’s washable, too, and Dupray offers replacement prefilters in different colors.

Sources indicate that the Bloom also has an AutoDetect mode that monitors air quality and adjusts the fan speed. There are three manual fan settings, along with a sleep mode for quieter operation. Dupray rates its lowest noise level at just 24 decibels, making it suitable for bedrooms and other living spaces where a loud fan would be distracting.

Recent findings suggest that it’s remarkably simple. The removable planter makes the HEPA filter accessible, and the fabric prefilter stretches on and off without clips or complicated fasteners.

In a recent development, another smart touch is the universal power adapter. It comes with interchangeable plug configurations for the U.S., U.K., and Europe. That’s not something I typically see included with an air purifier.

Industry observers note that my only complaint—and it’s minor—is the digital control display. The symbols for Auto, Sleep, and the fan-speed bars looked slightly blurry to me. I could still identify them and operate the purifier, but a sharper display would have been easier to read. Or I might need a new prescription for glasses.

At $249.99, the Bloom isn’t the cheapest way to get HEPA filtration, but its design sets it apart from the usual boxy models. It’s particularly appealing for living rooms, bedrooms, and home offices where an ordinary air purifier might detract from the decor.

Dupray advertises coverage up to 1,517 square feet, but that’s based on just one air change per hour. For more frequent air cleaning, it’s rated to cover 316 square feet at 4.8 air changes per hour. I’d use that smaller figure when choosing where to place it.

The Bloom also offers an optional wood tabletop model for anyone who prefers an accent table instead of a planter.

I love having a living plant incorporated into an appliance I’d otherwise try to hide. The Bloom is one of the few air purifiers I’ve tested that I’d happily put on display.

Breaking: Rule 14a-8: Perhaps Slow-Walking Recission is Best

💡 Key Takeaways
