    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that (Geneva, November 24, 2026) – New use, production, and acquisition of antipersonnel landmines contributed to killing or injuring at least 6,929 people in 2025, which is the highest annual total since 2020, Human Rights Watch said today with the release of the “Landmine Monitor 2026” by the International Campaign to Ban Landmines. Human Rights Watch is a founding member of the campaign and contributed to the report.

    Recent findings suggest that the 200-page report examines global compliance with the 1997 Mine Ban Treaty and the challenges facing the treaty nearly three decades after its adoption. The treaty comprehensively bans antipersonnel mines and commits countries to eliminate stockpiled weapons, clear contaminated land, and assist mine victims and affected communities.

    It has been revealed that “At a time when civilian casualties are rising and latest technologies make mines easier to deploy, supporting the Mine Ban Treaty is more notable than ever,” said Verity Coyle, deputy crisis, conflict and arms director at Human Rights Watch. “All countries should join the treaty, and members should fully uphold its obligations.”.

    Industry observers note that antipersonnel mines continue to kill and maim civilians long after fighting moves elsewhere. Whether they are placed by soldiers on the ground or delivered remotely by weapons systems and drones, the mines contaminate land, roads, and communities for years. Their presence can prevent displaced families from returning home, obstruct humanitarian operations, and undermine efforts to rebuild livelihoods and food production.

    It has been revealed that A total of 162 countries are now bound by the Mine Ban Treaty. Three countries joined during the reporting period: Lebanon, Marshall Islands, and Tonga. Five other countries withdrew from the treaty in 2025 and 2026: Estonia, Finland, Latvia, Lithuania, and Poland.

    According to recent reports, ukraine unveiled on July 18, 2025, that it would “suspend the operation” of the treaty while engaged in armed conflict with Russia, citing Russia’s extensive use of landmines. Suspensions, however, are unlawful under the treaty, notably during armed conflict, and Ukraine remains fully bound by all the treaty’s obligations. During the reporting period, Ukraine has acquired, produced, and used newly assembled antipersonnel mines, including types that are delivered by drone, in violation of the treaty.

    In addition to Ukraine’s use of antipersonnel mines, states not party to the treaty used them, including Iran, Myanmar, North Korea, and Russia.

    Antipersonnel mines were increasingly used in border conflicts, involving Cambodia and Thailand, Bangladesh and Myanmar, and in Thailand along the borders with Myanmar and Malaysia. Non-state armed groups also used antipersonnel mines, in many cases improvised, in Colombia, India, Myanmar, Pakistan, Sudan, and in locations in Western and Central Africa, including in the Chad Basin, Burkina Faso, and Mali.

    The Landmine Monitor reported that 15 states not party to the treaty either presently produce antipersonnel mines or maintain the option to produce them in the future. Of these, India, Myanmar, Poland, Russia, and South Korea appear to be actively producing or developing antipersonnel mines. Finland, Latvia, and Lithuania—all of which withdrew from the treaty in 2025—have indicated their intent to develop or acquire antipersonnel mines. Non-state armed groups have produced improvised mines that explode due to the presence, proximity, or contact of a person in Colombia, India, Africa’s Sahel region, and sporadically in Thailand.

    Sources indicate that in 2025, casualties from antipersonnel landmines and explosive remnants of war occurred in at least 54 countries and areas. Of these, 39 are party to the Mine Ban Treaty. Myanmar, which is not a party, recorded the highest number of annual casualties (1,891) for the third consecutive year, and Syria recorded 1,602 casualties. Civilians made up at least 84 percent (5,078) of all recorded casualties, while children accounted for 50 percent (1,690) of civilian casualties where the age group was known.

    Even as renewed mine use is contaminating latest territory, progress remains possible. Croatia declared completion of its mine clearance obligations in March 2026, following Oman in 2025. Since the Mine Ban Treaty entered into force in 1999, 32 states parties have successfully cleared all known antipersonnel mine contamination from their territory.

    The near elimination of government stockpiles remains one of the treaty’s greatest achievements. Of the 162 states parties, 157 report that they do not possess stockpiled antipersonnel mines. Ninety-four countries have finished destroying their stocks, a total of more than 55 million mines. As during previous reporting periods, Greece and Ukraine continue to possess stockpiles of antipersonnel mines, in violation of article 4 of the treaty.

    “The world should be moving closer to ending the suffering caused by antipersonnel mines, not witnessing a resurgence in their use,” Coyle noted. “Governments should be seeking global adoption of the ban treaty and reinforcing compliance, not stepping away from one of the world’s most successful humanitarian disarmament treaties.”.

    The “Landmine Monitor 2026” is the 28th annual publication by the International Campaign to Ban Landmines, the global coalition of nongovernmental organizations that received the 1997 Nobel Peace Prize. Human Rights Watch co-founded the campaign in 1992 and contributes to its Landmine Monitor reporting initiative.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (Brussels) – Companies that receive complaints of forced labor in their operations or supply chains should make sure affected workers have access to full and effective remedies, Human Rights Watch and a group of civil society organizations and trade unions said in a report released today.

    In the White Paper on Remediation of Forced Labour in the Private Economy, the organizations set out what appropriate and effective remedies look like for workers, and the concrete steps companies should take to deliver it.

    It has been revealed that “Forced labor does not end when a product is pulled from the shelves but only when workers who were trapped by debt, deceived, or threatened get their wages, documents, and dignity back,” mentioned Hélène de Rengervé, senior advocate at Human Rights Watch. “Companies should remedy labor abuses in their supply chains and engage with workers from the start to define appropriate solutions.”.

    It has been revealed that the groups propose concrete steps for companies to prepare, deliver and assess their remediation obligations. The report comes as the European Union prepares to enforce its Forced Labour Regulation, which will ban products made with forced labor from the EU market across all sectors and stages of production beginning on December 14, 2027. Under the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive, companies in its scope will also have a legal duty to remedy harm they cause, completely or in part.

    An estimated 17.3 million people were in situations of forced labor in the private economy in 2022, according to global estimates by the International Labour Organization (ILO), Walk Free, and the International Organization for Migration. The number of victims increased by 8 percent between 2016 and 2021. The ILO estimates that forced labor in the private economy generates US$63.9 billion in illegal profits every year.

    Academics and experts found that forced labor is rarely only the result of a few bad actors, but is rooted in poverty, discrimination, weak labor protections, and restrictive migration regimes. Migrant workers face heightened risks, including recruitment fees that lead to debt bondage, deceptive recruitment practices, and visas tied to a single employer. Fear of deportation and retaliation often keeps victims from seeking redress.

    In a recent development, the civil society groups remarked that companies should put in place remediation measures that restore as much as possible the situation for workers if the abuse had not occurred. This would require the cessation of the abuse, restitution, rehabilitation, compensation, apologies, and guarantees of non-repetition. Companies should also ensure that workers and their representatives can identify abuses through grievance mechanisms they trust, define remedies, and assess whether they have been delivered to their satisfaction, the groups said. At all times, affected workers should be protected from retaliation.

    In a recent development, companies should treat remediation as part of their human rights due diligence, not as a one-off response to a scandal, the groups mentioned. Their responsibility should reflect their involvement in failing to prevent or meaningfully address the harm. Companies should not “cut and run” from suppliers when and where labor abuses, including forced labor, is found, as this can leave workers worse off. Instead, the groups said, companies should fairly agree on how to address and share remediation costs.

    To prevent forced labor from occurring and recurring, companies should examine structural causes such as poverty, discrimination and impairments to freedom of association but also how their own purchasing practices may drive it. They should pay to cover the cost of decent working conditions and living wages. The groups point to worker-driven models, such as the Fair Food Program in US agriculture and the Dindigul Agreement in India’s textile sector, as evidence of good practices.

    The EU and its member states should ensure that the competent authorities empowered to enforce the Forced Labour Regulation assess whether effective remediation has actually delivered for workers, including through workers’ own accounts and evidence of compensation paid. They should also ensure that, regardless of their migration status, workers can at least access support, file complaints, and recover unpaid wages.

    “Workers know best what they have lost and what it will take to rebuild their lives,” de Rengervé mentioned. “Companies and EU authorities should listen to affected workers and measure the efficiency of remediation by what workers receive and whether they completely remediate the harm suffered.”.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, from Magistrate Judge Virginia DeMarchi (N.D. Cal.) today in Doe 1 v. U.S.:.

    Plaintiffs … filed this action against the United States, Google LLC ("Google"), and X.AI Corp. ("X.AI"). Plaintiffs sue for themselves and on behalf of a proposed class of "[a]ll Jeffrey Epstein victims whose private information, including their name, photographic image, telephone number, email address, physical address, or place of residence, was disclosed without their consent in unredacted documents released by the United States between December 2025 and the present." Plaintiffs also sue on behalf of an injunctive relief subclass of "[a]ll Class members whose disclosed private information is indexed, cached, hosted, or otherwise made available to the public through any service operated by the United States, Google, or [X.AI]." The subclass "seeks injunctive relief under Rules 23(b)(2) only.".

    Plaintiffs allege that in "late 2025 and early 2026, the U.S. Department of Justice ('DOJ') outed approximately 100 victims of the convicted sexual predator, publishing their private information and identifying them to the world." Plaintiffs further allege that "[e]ven after the government acknowledged the disclosure violated the rights of the victims and withdrew most of the information, artificial intelligence products like Google's AI Mode and [X.]AI's Grok, continue to republish it, refusing victims' pleas to take it down." Plaintiffs' sole claim against the United States is for violation of the Privacy Act of 1974 ("Privacy Act"), 5 U.S.C. § 552a(b) and § 552(g)(1)(D). Plaintiffs assert several claims under California law and common law against both Google and X.AI for violation of California's Unfair Competition Law (Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17200, et seq.), invasion of privacy, negligence, and negligent infliction of emotional distress. Plaintiffs seek injunctive relief, compensatory damages, statutory damages, punitive damages, reasonable attorneys' fees and costs, as well as pre- and post-judgment interest.

    The Court rejected the federal government's motion to dismiss (Google and X.AI's motion to dismiss will be considered later):.

    Recent findings suggest that "The Privacy Act prohibits a federal agency from disclosing a record contained in a system of records pertaining to an individual unless the individual requests the information or consents to the disclosure in writing." To state a claim for wrongful disclosure under the Privacy Act, a plaintiff must allege facts showing that (1) the information disclosed is contained in a system of records; (2) the agency improperly disclosed the information; (3) the disclosure had an adverse effect on the plaintiff; (3) the disclosure was willful or intentional; and (4) the plaintiff suffered actual damages. The Privacy Act "provides for damages only where 'the court determines that the agency acted in a manner which was intentional or willful.'".

    Sources indicate that for the present purpose of resolving the United States' motion to dismiss, only the third element regarding "willful or intentional" disclosure is at matter. Under the Privacy Act, willful or intentional conduct is "only somewhat greater than gross negligence," and "the Privacy Act 'imposes liability only when the agency acts in violation of the Act in a willful or intentional manner, either by committing the act without grounds for believing it to be lawful, or flagrantly disregarding others' rights under the Act.'" ….

    In a recent development, the United States notes that the disclosures in question were made pursuant to the Epstein Files Transparency Act ("EFTA"), which required the DOJ to release, within a 30-day period, millions of pages of documents from the DOJ's investigation of Mr. Epstein. While acknowledging that DOJ "admittedly made some mistakes, including inadvertent disclosures of victim information," the United States indicates that in enacting the EFTA, Congress imposed an "unprecedented" and "herculean task" upon the DOJ.

    Additionally, the United States states that the DOJ made remedial efforts by, for example, establishing "a website through which victims could confidentially notify the [DOJ] of information that required additional redaction." In these circumstances, the United States argues that plaintiffs' allegations cannot, as a matter of law, meet the "'high hurdle'" for the requisite willful or intentional conduct….

    Plaintiffs maintain that the FAC alleges sufficient facts plausibly supporting willful or intentional conduct, including allegations that the DOJ (1) prioritized "maximum transparency" and the rapid release of information over victims' privacy interests; (2) refused victims' requests to remove the subject information, or did not respond to such requests; and (3) acted out of retaliatory motives and released files as "a punitive response to victims' public advocacy for transparency, effectively 'doxxing' victims who spoke out by exposing their identities and contact information.".

    Sources indicate that the question of whether an agency has acted without grounds for believing the act to be lawful or has acted in flagrant disregard of others' rights under the Privacy Act depends on the context of the disclosure in each case and is a fact-intensive inquiry. Indeed, in its reply, the United States asserts that the conduct in question is measured on a continuum. If that is the case, then the United States' assertion only bolsters the conclusion that there is no "bright line" defining "willful" or "intentional" conduct, and that such matters often are not conducive to determination as a matter of law at the pleading stage….

    Viewing the facts in the light most favorable to plaintiffs, and drawing all reasonable inferences in their favor, as is required at this stage of the proceedings, the Court finds that plaintiffs have sufficiently pled facts plausibly supporting their claim that DOJ willfully or intentionally violated their rights under the Privacy Act. While the United States maintains that the mere presence of an error or mistake is not indicative of an intentional Privacy Act violation, the Court need not adopt the government's characterization of plaintiffs' allegations.

    In essence, plaintiffs allege that the DOJ's disclosure of the subject materials was a "deliberate policy choice" to prioritize DOJ's obligations under the EFTA over its obligations and victims' rights under the Privacy Act. For pleading purposes, those allegations appear plausible, and are not inconsistent with the United States' assertion that DOJ was faced with a "herculean task" to accomplish within "an impossible-to-execute time frame." … [P]laintiffs' allegations that the DOJ made a deliberate decision, as a matter of policy, to give priority to its obligations under the EFTA ahead of those under the Privacy Act, are sufficient to support a plausible claim for relief….

    According to recent reports, elizabeth Antonia Kramer, Julie C. Erickson, and Kevin M. Osborne (Erickson Kramer Osborne LLP) represent plaintiffs.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    November 18, 2026, 12:42 pm CST.

    A judge in Michigan was found guilty Monday of drunk driving after he rear-ended a public transit bus, but a district court judge ruled that prosecutors failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that his blood alcohol level met the state’s threshold for intoxication. (Image from Shutterstock).

    A judge in Michigan was found guilty Monday of drunk driving after he rear-ended a public transit bus, but a district court judge ruled that prosecutors failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that his blood alcohol level met the threshold for the state’s original charge of a more serious offense.

    Warren 37th District Court Chief Judge John M. Chmura, 63, was found guilty of intoxication while driving his Ford Fusion into a parked bus that was displaying hazard lights March 25. But the court rejected the charge of Chmura driving with an elevated high blood alcohol content of 0.17 or greater, according to coverage on Law360.

    Novi 52nd District Court Judge David Law noted that Chmura’s judgment had been affected, but he questioned the blood alcohol concentration at the time of the crash.

    Sources indicate that “This court may think it knows the answer to whether or not this was a high BAC case,” Law noted. “But thinking it knows is not enough. It needs to be proven beyond a reasonable doubt.”.

    Industry observers note that A bus driver sitting inside the bus waiting to resume his route was uninjured in the crash. Sterling Heights, Michigan, police officer Jonathan Journeau testified that Chmura smelled of alcohol, slurred his speech and couldn’t maintain his balance.

    Recent findings suggest that chmura’s attorney, David J. Kramer of the David J. Kramer Law Firm, argued that prosecutors could not establish the higher offense because Journeau failed to determine when the judge’s final alcoholic beverage was consumed.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • When Pakistani senators visited the prototype Islamabad Model Jail on November 19 and inspected the healthcare facilities that would be available to prisoners, they called them “adequate.” But the conditions they observed on their curated tour are a far cry from the reality most prisoners experience in Pakistan’s justice system.
    • Human Rights Watch has documented structural and systemic problems in Pakistan’s jails and prisons that leave most inmates with little access to health care.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When Pakistani senators visited the prototype Islamabad Model Jail on November 19 and inspected the healthcare facilities that would be available to prisoners, they called them “adequate.” But the conditions they observed on their curated tour are a far cry from the reality most prisoners experience in Pakistan’s justice system.

    Human Rights Watch has documented structural and systemic problems in Pakistan’s jails and prisons that leave most inmates with little access to health care. Many inmates who fall ill in custody fail to receive prompt or decent care at all.

    After two prisoners died in Peshawar Central Prison following alleged delays in medical treatment, a lawyer petitioned the Peshawar High Court asking that prisons across the province be required to record when prisoners request medical help and establish clear procedures for emergency hospital transfers.

    Colonial-era laws have long-enabled Pakistani officials and powerful people to interfere in prison operations, sometimes making use of poor conditions to harass jailed political opponents. In a November 16 letter released by his lawyer, former Prime Minister Imran Khan appealed for urgent medical care for himself and his wife, Bushra Bibi, citing his high blood pressure and her need for eye surgery. Khan’s appeal echoes complaints about medical care in custody from former President Asif Ali Zardari and former Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif. All have alleged that prison services denied access to medical care as a form of punishment.

    Federal and provincial governments in Pakistan should bring health care in jails and prisons in line with international standards, notably the United Nations Standard Minimum Rules for the Treatment of Prisoners (the Mandela Rules), which require that prisoners receive necessary free medical care to the same standard available in the community, with prompt attention in emergencies. In October, Justice Project Pakistan called for common standards across provinces so prisoners can see medical specialists when needed and continue treatment after release.

    According to recent reports, pakistan’s federal and provincial governments should provide prescribed medicines free of charge and require prisons to record how long patients wait for care. When care requires an urgent hospital transfer, prison authorities should promptly facilitate transport. Authorities should ensure all prisoners, regardless of political affiliation or status, receive timely and adequate medical care, with continuity of treatment.

    #193108. Philippines: As ICC Tries Duterte, Stalled Justice at Home

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3184 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hrw ↗ Open Full Page

    Philippines: As ICC Tries Duterte, Stalled Justice at Home

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3184 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hrw

    ⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, (Manila) – Philippine authorities have failed to investigate extrajudicial killings in the “war on drugs” since former President Rodrigo Duterte was transferred to the International Criminal Court for prosecution, Human Rights Watch remarked today.
    • Industry observers note that president Ferdinand Marcos Jr., who took office in June 2022, pledged to pursue prosecutions of Duterte-era “drug war” killings and established a Justice Department task force for the purpose, but only four cases have reached the courts.
    • “President Marcos’ pledge to hold police accountable for past and ongoing abuses in its anti-drug campaign has been a failure,” said Lian Buan, Southeast Asia researcher at Human Rights Watch.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, (Manila) – Philippine authorities have failed to investigate extrajudicial killings in the “war on drugs” since former President Rodrigo Duterte was transferred to the International Criminal Court for prosecution, Human Rights Watch remarked today. The ICC trial in The Hague against Duterte for crimes against humanity is scheduled to begin on November 30, 2026.

    Industry observers note that president Ferdinand Marcos Jr., who took office in June 2022, pledged to pursue prosecutions of Duterte-era “drug war” killings and established a Justice Department task force for the purpose, but only four cases have reached the courts. Families of victims seeking to file fresh cases face significant barriers. Meanwhile, government records and human rights group reports show that drug-war abuses continue, with police harassing, arbitrarily arresting, and at times killing suspected drug dealers and users.

    “President Marcos’ pledge to hold police accountable for past and ongoing abuses in its anti-drug campaign has been a failure,” said Lian Buan, Southeast Asia researcher at Human Rights Watch. “The Philippine government needs to prioritize justice for all drug-war victims and provide their families’ adequate redress.”.

    Recent findings suggest that between September and November 2026, Human Rights Watch interviewed 13 people, including 7 drug-war victims and their families both under Duterte and Marcos, 4 human rights defenders, and 2 government officials; reviewed recent data and reporting on drug-related killings; and analyzed a database of local government Peace and Order and Public Safety Looks. Human Rights Watch also requested and received information from the Philippine Justice Department and Commission on Human Rights on drug-war cases before the courts.

    It has been revealed that relatives of drug-war victims described a justice system in which the burden of uncovering evidence of an unlawful killing fell mostly on them instead of government prosecutors. “It’s so hard to prove that you’re telling the truth,” stated a woman whose husband was killed in 2016 in a police “buy-bust” drug sting operation. “It’s tiring pursuing a case here—it’s as if we can never pass the tests.”.

    Recent findings suggest that some facing obstacles to justice have pinned their hopes on the ICC. “In the Philippines, what was our chance, given how the government works,” stated another woman whose husband was killed by unidentified assailants in 2016. “In the ICC they are impartial, that’s where our hope is.”.

    During the Duterte presidency from 2016 to 2022, the Philippine National Police reported 6,200 deaths during anti-drug operations, although United Nations agencies, the Philippine Commission on Human Rights, the Supreme Court, and domestic human rights groups put the number of killings by police and unidentified assailants at between 20,000 and 30,000.

    Only five cases of Duterte-era “drug war” killings, involving nine police officers, have resulted in convictions. Government prosecutors initiated the first three cases, following the successive murders of three teenage boys in Caloocan in August 2017, which sparked public outrage. The fourth and fifth cases—for killings in 2016—were filed through the efforts of nongovernmental legal groups and led to convictions in 2024 and 2025.

    In November 2024, the Justice Department created a task force to investigate and prosecute extrajudicial killings during Duterte’s “war on drugs” but only four cases it identified have advanced to trial, with three others under preliminary investigation, based on Justice Department data.

    Sources indicate that the Marcos administration, after arresting and surrendering Duterte to the ICC in March 2025, declared renewed efforts to advance domestic accountability for the “drug war.” But families and human rights groups who met with Justice Department officials said that they were concerned the government’s witness protection program would not keep their families safe if they pursued charges against police officers. Meetings between victims’ groups and the Justice Department tapered off.

    Industry observers note that duterte will stand trial at the ICC for three counts of crimes against humanity of murder and attempted murder allegedly committed when he was mayor of Davao City, and then president between November 2011 and March 2019. The prosecution’s case focuses on a non-exhaustive list of 56 specific incidents and 87 victims, while noting that “[its] evidence demonstrates that the attack [against a civilian population] was broader than this representative sample of incidents.”.

    According to recent reports, the ICC is a court of last resort, only stepping in when domestic authorities are unwilling or unable to investigate and prosecute crimes under its jurisdiction. In November 2021, the Duterte government asked the ICC prosecutor to defer his investigation, opened in September 2021, claiming that national authorities had begun their own drug-war investigations of extrajudicial killings.

    Recent findings suggest that in January 2023, ICC judges ruled that the Philippine government had failed to demonstrate that it took sufficient action to investigate and prosecute Duterte-era killings and authorized the resumption of the ICC prosecutor’s investigation. The decision was upheld on appeal.

    Industry observers note that the ICC trial against Duterte begins as the court is under growing pressure from the US government, which has vowed to dismantle the ICC “brick by brick.” On October 9, the Trump administration sanctioned the ICC, escalating its attack on the court and adding to existing sanctions on ICC judges and prosecutors, three Palestinian groups, and a UN human rights expert. The Trump administration sanctions reaffirm the ICC’s critical role as a court of last resort, Human Rights Watch stated.

    Marcos has never repudiated the “war on drugs” as a government policy and has yet to rescind the orders and other policy statements Duterte issued that underpinned the anti-drug campaign. In its review of a database of 2023-2025 local government budgets, Human Rights Watch found that 77 municipalities had allocated funds for anti-drug campaign awards and rewards, or for financial support to informants, police officials, and other local officials. Two of those municipalities, and another eight municipalities specifically referred to “neutralization” or “negation” of suspects; terms used as euphemisms for “killing” in 2016 police circular that set out the “war on drugs.” While such incentives are not necessarily unlawful, those linked to enforcement goals or operational results can create pressure to meet targets and encourage abusive practices, including extrajudicial killings.

    Despite a significant decline in drug-related extrajudicial killings during the Marcos administration, such killings and other abuses continue, particularly in low-income urban areas where they remain routine. As of November 7, there have been at least 1,342 public reports of drug-related killings under Marcos. These reports identified uniformed officers as responsible for 486 of those deaths.

    According to recent reports, the Philippine government’s failure to hold those responsible to account perpetuates a climate of impunity. Families of drug-war victims under the Marcos administration encounter many of the same past obstacles when seeking justice, but the Justice Department has no task force or special mechanism to investigate post-Duterte cases, Human Rights Watch said.

    Recent findings suggest that “Even if killings are down from the ghastly Duterte years, President Marcos’ pledged ‘bloodless campaign’ against drugs has been anything but bloodless,” Buan remarked. “To end these abuses, Marcos needs to stop the brutal ‘drug war’ and put in place a robust and impartial law enforcement and judicial system.”Elusive Justice for Killings during Duterte and Marcos Administrations.

    Under the Duterte administration in 2020, the Justice Department opened an inter-agency panel to “reinvestigate” drug-war killings by the police. The panel identified 52 cases in which the Philippine National Police carried out internalinvestigations. However, by 2024, when Marcos was in office, the panel had only filed six cases in court. In November 2024, the Justice Department created a newly introduced task force on Duterte-era drug war killings. It began investigations anew and worked mainly with the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI)—the Justice Department’s investigative arm—instead of with the police to avoid conflicts of interest when developing cases implicating police officers.

    Sources indicate that despite renewed Justice Department efforts, victims’ families still struggled to file charges. Many victims’ families who wanted to pursue charges could not do so because their relative’s death certificate declared an illness as the cause of death, even though they were found with gunshot wounds to their heads and bodies. During the height of Duterte’s “drug war,” police pressured families to sign waivers stating that they did not want to conduct autopsies or pursue charges, in exchange for faster retrievals of the bodies from funeral homes. Many families could not afford the autopsy fees, and without accurate government death records, they could not pursue charges.

    Industry observers note that the woman whose husband was killed in a police operation in 2016 decided in 2022 to retrieve documents about his killing from the police because she believed the climate of fear had lifted under Marcos. “They were not really helping us,” she noted. “They just left us there to search their logbooks.” Police officials had named the woman’s husband as a drug suspect killed in an “armed encounter” in a news report that featured her children wailing for their dead father. Yet she never found a police report of the operation, only a record of bystanders injured. She was unable to prove he was shot dead, because his death certificate lists the cause of death as pneumonia and his body was cremated. Government investigators have not pursued a case. The woman recalled the one conversation with the Justice Department: “They said, ‘If you have no document like police report or autopsy, it’s hard to file a case.’ So, what about me? I had no documents.”.

    The woman whose husband was killed by unidentified assailants did not know for years the circumstances under which her husband was killed. She found his body with gunshot wounds at a funeral home in 2016 and signed a waiver not to conduct an autopsy. His death certificate listed pneumonia as cause of death. After Marcos became president, the woman sought help from a nonprofit law group. In 2023, she had her husband’s body exhumed and examined by a forensic pathologist, Raquel Fortun. The autopsy showed that he died from gunshot wounds to the head.

    In a recent development, that year, she finally found the police report from the night her husband died. It stated that police responding to reports of gunshots found him dead with three sachets of crystal meth, and a piece of cardboard that read “I’m a drug pusher, don’t be like me.” She had an interview with the NBI, who told her they had also summoned local officials and the funeral home. But nothing further happened in the investigation. “No one has followed up with me, I still wonder what happened to that NBI case,” she said.

    Sources indicate that fortun became a commissioner of the Philippine Truth Commission, a civil society initiative working closely with the Catholic Church to investigate Duterte-era drug war crimes. She has recorded 13 cases in which people were shot and killed but whose death certificates cite illnesses such as heart attack, pneumonia, and high blood pressure as causes of death. Fortun noted during a Truth Commission briefing that government prosecutors have pushed back when presented with evidence of falsified death certificates in court. In one case, the government prosecutor acted on behalf of the defendant, instead of the victim: “I was grilled in cross-examination, and I was surprised that it was the prosecutor. I don’t understand it. So if you’re a poor family with a similar case, would you still have it corrected. It’s so hard.”.

    Sources indicate that the Commission on Human Rights told Human Rights Watch that its investigations of Duterte-era drug-war killings have resulted in cases moving through the justice system. Between 2016 and 2023, 25 cases were filed in court, 37 cases at the Office of the Ombudsman, and 42 with the Justice Department. No further progress was reported by the commission on the cases filed. The commission has no prosecutorial power and can only file cases in a manner similar to private complainants.

    Sources indicate that despite the Commission on Human Right’s limited powers, families seek confirmation from the commission that they have been victims of rights violations, which entitles them to limited financial assistance under the commission’s internal rules of procedure. Yet the commission denied assistance for lack of evidence to two women whose husbands were fatally shot in 2016.

    Recent findings suggest that only the woman who exhumed her husband’s body was able to challenge the decision; after she submitted the postmortem examination report in August 2026, the commission told her to file a petition for reinvestigation. “I just want to prove that what I’m saying is the truth,” she stated.

    The commission told Human Rights Watch that it created its own task force, which is currently reinvestigating 493 cases of Duterte-era drug-war killings, with the goal of resolving 140 before the end of 2026.

    Duterte-Era Drug-War Policy Persists.

    The mother of a man killed by police in Central Luzon in 2022—after Marcos became president—noted that she tried to pursue murder charges. She cited a witness who told her that her son was lured to the location the night of the killing, and an autopsy report that indicated he had been shot execution-style and not during an armed encounter as police had claimed. The witness has since gone missing. Prosecutors dismissed her case twice, most recently in 2025, because a medical expert’s testimony was required. The mother said that she was working on finding a medical expert to testify, but even just the cost of reproducing copies of documents was weighing on her.

    It has been revealed that no special task force has been created to investigate alleged drug-war crimes under the Marcos government. The government has claimed that its anti-drug campaign is “bloodless” and that “rather than resorting to violence, it focuses on strengthening prevention and rehabilitation efforts.” But Human Rights Watch found that disturbing Duterte-era language, such as “neutralization,” remains in prepares for current anti-drugs campaigns.

    There is no legal definition of “neutralization,” but on July 1, 2016, Duterte’s police chief, Ronald Dela Rosa, issued Command Memorandum Circular 16-2016, the operational document for the anti-drug campaign, instructing police officers to “neutralize” suspected criminals.

    In a recent development, in 2017, two human rights groups, the Center for International Law (CenterLaw) and the Free Legal Assistance Group (FLAG), filed petitions before the Supreme Court seeking to declare the anti-drug campaign unconstitutional, citing the use of the word “neutralization” in the circular. The Supreme Court has yet to rule on the case. ICC prosecutors have accused Duterte of developing “a State policy to ‘neutralize’ through violent crimes, including murder, alleged criminals in the Philippines who were perceived or alleged to be involved in drug-related and other crimes,” noting the language in the circular.

    According to recent reports, in November 2025, the ICC issued a sealed arrest warrant for Dela Rosa. He is alleged to be responsible for the crime against humanity of murder as part of a common plan together with other co-perpetrators—including Duterte—with the aim of killing drug suspects between 2011 and 2019. This included issuing the Command Memorandum Circular 16-2016, instructing police officers to “neutralize” suspected criminals. The ICC unsealed the warrant in May 2026; Dela Rosa has since gone into hiding.

    The Marcos government has not rescinded that circular, but in 2024 the Philippine National Police told lawmakers that they were actually following a upcoming circular without the word “neutralize.” The Marcos government also committed todrug policy reform as part of a US$4 million joint human rights program with the United Nations.

    Sources indicate that A 2026 study by two organizations, No Box Philippines and Harm Reduction International, found that the Philippine government was still allocating millions of US dollars for local anti-drug campaigns whose policy documents retained similar language to the original circular, such as “neutralization” and “negation.” Their findings were based on an analysis of 2023-2025 local government “Peace and Order and Public Safety” budgets. Local governments are supervised by the Department of Interior and Local Government, the executive department that also supervises the police.

    Human Rights Watch analyzed local government intends obtained by the two groups, and found that 85 towns, municipalities, and cities allocated funds for rewards, awards, and incentives for successful anti-drug operations, including 10 municipalities where the funds were specifically for “conducting negation operations” or “neutralizing drug personalities.”.

    During the Duterte presidency, for an area to declare itself “drug-free,” local councils had to monitor, surveil, and compile a drug “watch list.” Human rights groups frequently alleged the lists determined who would be killed, whether the assailants were police officers or masked police agents.

    Under public safety prepares in effect under Marcos, local governments still offer financial rewards for making their areas “drug-free,” by giving “incentives to assets,” or “awards/rewards for significant illegal drugs accomplishment” or “neutralization of drug personalities.” ICC prosecutors alleged in their case against Duterte that “law enforcement personnel knew that extrajudicial killings would result in them being financially rewarded.” There have been fewer drug-related killings under Marcos, but human rights defenders who live in drug-war hotspots in Metro Manila and neighboring provinces stated abuses continued.

    Recent findings suggest that “Their raids are not as brazen, but they still plant evidence,” one rights defender mentioned. The quota system—the number of arrests and kills under Duterte to qualify for rewards—“was still alive.”.

    Under Marcos, human rights defenders monitoring drug-war abuses in their communities have observed that the police are more likely to extort victims than to kill them, targeting many of the same people who were on drug “watch lists.” They remarked police still arbitrarily arrest people, threaten them with drug charges, and then detain them on criminal anti-street-gambling charges with lighter penalties. The Philippine organization PhilRights has documented that “police officers offer to cover the victims’ release costs in exchange for repayment with interest, effectively profiting from the arrest.”.

    According to recent reports, in 2025, a man came home one night to find police officers in the vicinity, his sister said. “They patted him down and found nothing,” she said. “But a police informant handed sachets of crystal meth and forced him to admit it was his.” The police arrested the man and took his bicycle. She said she made several visits to the police station where her brother had been detained. The police officials told her he had been charged with gambling. “I told them, ‘You said you found drugs, now the charge is gambling. How long are you detaining him?’” she said. “They told us we can ‘just pay P10,000 [$160].’ But we had no money at all at the time.”.

    In a recent development, the sister took a month processing documents in several police stations before her brother was released. He was detained for a month without being brought before a judge in violation of his rights. “We can still see them surveilling our area from time to time,” the sister mentioned.

    Philippine Police Killings in Duterte’s “War on Drugs”.

    Death Squad Killings in Tagum City, Philippines.

    #193105. Beyond Lupin: The Brazen Gentlemen Thieves of Fiction

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    Beyond Lupin: The Brazen Gentlemen Thieves of Fiction

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1106 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Assane Diop has no use for weapons or threats as he plunders Parisian homes and museums.
    • He models his stylish crimes on the escapades of Arsène Lupin, the top-hatted, monocle-wearing creation of French novelist Maurice Leblanc.
    • Recent findings suggest that diop’s caper-filled quest for justice made the show one of Netflix’s most successful foreign-made franchises by the time it went on hiatus in the fall of 2023.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Assane Diop has no use for weapons or threats as he plunders Parisian homes and museums. His meticulously planned heists are executed with a showman’s flair. The anti-hero of the hit Netflix series Lupin, portrayed to perfection by actor Omar Sy, Diop dons elaborate disguises, slips into fake identities, and turns on the charm as he swipes priceless gems and outwits the police.

    He models his stylish crimes on the escapades of Arsène Lupin, the top-hatted, monocle-wearing creation of French novelist Maurice Leblanc. Lupin made his debut in 1905, at the height of the glamorous Belle Époque, and was featured in two dozen novels and short story collections. A skilled burglar and a master of disguise, this impish shapeshifter relishes the challenge of stealing the un-stealable and often returns the treasures he pilfers. He’s more interested in righting wrongs than living off ill-gotten gains. So is Diop – he’s determined to exonerate his father, who was wrongly accused of stealing a priceless necklace from the powerful and corrupt businessman Hubert Pellegrini.

    Recent findings suggest that diop’s caper-filled quest for justice made the show one of Netflix’s most successful foreign-made franchises by the time it went on hiatus in the fall of 2023. As Lupin returns for a long-anticipated fourth season, here’s a lineup of five of the slickest gentlemen thieves of fiction:.

    A.J. Raffles: Lupin was France’s answer to a wildly popular English thief of fiction. In 1898, E. W. Hornung (the brother-in-law of Arthur Conan Doyle) published the first of twenty-six stories on the adventures of Arthur Raffles, a London man-about-town and star cricket player who steals to support his expensive lifestyle and keep up appearances. His speciality is cracking safes and he enlists a sidekick from his school days, Bunny Manders, as a partner-in-crime.

    Despite his crooked side-gig, Raffles adheres to a gentlemanly moral code. He shudders at the thought of preying on a host or a friend, and rarely packs a gun when he sets out to steal. “It would be very awkward if anything went wrong,” he tells Manders. “One might use it, and that’s not the game at all.” He stalks the corrupt and the obscenely wealthy, reasoning that “the immorally rich” are the logical targets for a “richly immoral” thief like himself.

    In a recent development, hercule Flambeau: His name may sound like that of a certain Belgian detective, but Flambeau’s obsession is stealing jewels, not solving crimes. That changes after a run-in with a priest and part-time detective dreamed up by writer G.K. Chesterton. In the first Father Brown short story, “The Blue Cross,” published in 1910, the clergyman with a kindly demeanor and a keen sense of human nature foils Flambeau’s attempt to steal a religious relic.

    Like Lupin, Flambeau is one of France’s most-wanted criminals – Chesterton described him as a “colossus of crime” with a long record of “ingenious and wholesale robbery.” And like Lupin, he can disguise himself and hide in plain sight, despite being over six feet tall. He is also “a startling acrobat,” wrote his creator, who “could leap like a grasshopper and melt into the tree-tops like a monkey.” Flambeau became a recurring character, appearing in more than a dozen of the fifty-three Father Brown stories, and not only reforms but eventually helps the clergyman to crack cases.

    Sources indicate that john Robie: It’s the early 1950s on the French Riviera and Robie, a wily burglar whose agility earned him the nickname “Le Chat” before he was caught and imprisoned, is forced out of retirement when a copycat makes him a suspect in newly introduced crimes. The protagonist in American travel writer David Dodge’s 1952 novel To Catch a Thief sets out to trap his doppelgänger.

    Robie is the consummate gentleman thief – dashing, clever, a master of his calling. Who better to portray him when Alfred Hitchcock brought the story to the big screen in 1955 than the king of suave, Cary Grant. “For what it’s worth,” Grant-as-Robie points out in a line added for the movie, “I never stole from anybody who would go hungry.”.

    Sources indicate that sir Charles Lytton: Peter Sellers’s hilariously inept Inspector Jacques Clouseau debuted in the 1963 movie The Pink Panther, but the real star of the blockbuster franchise’s first instalment was David Niven. He was cast as the debonaire playboy Sir Charles Lytton, who leads a double life as an elusive jewel thief known as “The Phantom.” Niven was an inspired choice – he played Raffles on screen in 1939, in one of many films to feature Hornung’s character.

    The Pink Panther is reputed to be the world’s largest diamond and Lytton has come to a ski resort in the Italian Alps to steal it. The bumbling Clouseau is there to try to stop him. Niven may have enjoyed top billing as a classy crook but Sellers’s over-the-top performance stole the show and hijacked the franchise.

    Recent findings suggest that danny Ocean: Frank Sinatra was the first to tackle the role of the ringleader of a gang of thieves who rob five Las Vegas casinos on New Year’s Eve in the 1960 movie Ocean’s 11. George Clooney revived the character four decades later in 2001’s Ocean’s Eleven, with Danny assembling a team of skilled crooks (an all-star cast that includes Brad Pitt and Matt Damon) to loot a supposedly impregnable Vegas vault.

    According to recent reports, the movie inspired two sequels, with the gang reuniting to steal a Fabergé egg in Ocean’s Twelve and a casino’s cash and a trove of diamonds in Ocean’s Thirteen. In each movie the targets are fellow thieves or ruthless, unscrupulous moguls. The heists are filled with Lupin-worthy disguises and deceptions and Clooney is a natural for the modern iteration of the cool, classy crook.

    It’s little wonder the gentleman thief is a staple of fiction. His victims are fellow travellers who deserve to be cut down to size, or have insurance policies or pockets deep enough to absorb their losses. Admiring their audacity and cheering them on is a guilty pleasure we can all enjoy.

    It has been revealed that dean Jobb’s latest true crime book, A Gentleman and a Thief: The Daring Jewel Heists of a Jazz Age Rogue (Algonquin Books and HarperCollins Canada), is a Latest York Times Editors’ Choice and a national bestseller in Canada. It’s the story of Arthur Barry, who charmed the elite of 1920s New York City while planning and executing some of the most brazen jewel thefts in history. Find him at deanjobb.com.

    #193104. Who supervises the system? Agentic AI and the future of lawyer oversight

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1278 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Abajournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Who supervises the system? Agentic AI and the future of lawyer oversight

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1278 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Abajournal

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, by Scott A.
    • Recent findings suggest that for two years, the legal profession’s artificial intelligence conversation has centered on an attorney asking a system a question and checking its answer.
    • Recent findings suggest that systems entering legal practice perform work: taking in a matter, researching, drafting motions, and choosing their own next steps.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, by Scott A. Meyers and Michael Adler.

    Recent findings suggest that for two years, the legal profession’s artificial intelligence conversation has centered on an attorney asking a system a question and checking its answer. That is no longer enough.

    Recent findings suggest that systems entering legal practice perform work: taking in a matter, researching, drafting motions, and choosing their own next steps. Used well, they can reduce routine work, freeing lawyers for judgment and client advice.

    According to recent reports, the profession built its supervision framework around people and bounded tools. An agentic system fits neither model: It has no license to lose or judgment to train, yet acts across a workflow with autonomy the Model Rules do not squarely address.

    When AI moves from answering questions to executing multistep legal workflows, what does meaningful human oversight look like?

    The unit of supervision is no longer an answer; it is a system of delegated decisions.

    It has been revealed that the ABA Model Rules of Professional Conduct anticipated part of this shift. In 2012, the ABA changed Rule 5.3’s title from “Responsibilities Regarding Nonlawyer Assistants” to “Responsibilities Regarding Nonlawyer Assistance.” Its comments encompassed technology-enabled services; a companion resolution added technological competence to what became Comment 8 of Rule 1.1. In 2024, Formal Opinion 512 applied Rules 1.1, 5.1, and 5.3 to lawyers’ use of generative AI and their supervision of the people and providers using it.

    Recent findings suggest that that guidance remains organized around a tool: review its output, protect client information, train customers and assess providers. It offers less direction when the system executes the workflow, deciding which documents to pull, which facts matter, and what goes where—decisions the finished product may not reveal. Reviewing only the output confirms the car arrived, not its route. Supervision of output is not supervision of process.

    METR’s May 2026 report sharpens the point. Assessing agents inside frontier developers (or entities that train AI models), it found them exceeding intended bounds and misleading consumers about their work, especially on difficult tasks. It did not study law firm deployments, and routine monitoring might have caught every incident because an independent record existed. The lesson: A lawyer cannot treat an agent’s account as the record of its work. That account is another output of the same probabilistic process, which has training incentives that can reward telling users what they want to hear. Asking the agent to double-check itself is not an independent control.

    It has been revealed that accountability cannot rest solely with whoever pressed “run.” It must be institutional and individual, extending to those who designed, approved and maintained the workflow. Every deployed workflow should have a named lawyer-owner authorized to pause it, just as every matter has a responsible partner. This does not displace the matter lawyer’s responsibilities. The owner’s authority must permit suspension on suspicion alone before a committee convenes or a vendor responds. Ownership without it is a label.

    In a recent development, final output review remains necessary. Oversight must also cover consequential junctures: privilege calls, external communications, filings and anything irreversible or beyond client authorization. Supervision begins at design time: deciding what a workflow may do independently, its latitude to reason, and where it must stop and ask. Every firm should be able to answer: Where can this system act without a human seeing it first, and who decided that?

    A tested record on comparable work can justify less intensive routine checking, though never at those consequential junctures. Greater autonomy should be approved and recorded. Material changes to the model, tools, permissions or workflow should trigger reassessment and renewed authorization.

    Autonomy bundles three permissions requiring separate calibration: generating work product, accessing sensitive information, and acting in firm or client systems. Permissions should narrow as consequences grow: broad room to draft; matter-scoped room to read; and narrow, logged room to act. A first-year may draft the memo; nobody gives them unilateral wire authority. The grant of action is never implied by the grant of access.

    It has been revealed that if a firm cannot trace what a system did, it cannot supervise it; where reasoning cannot be audited, behavior must be. Otherwise, recordkeeping, preservation, and verification of representations to clients, courts, and third parties may suffer. Three mechanisms matter: an audit trail independent of the agent’s reporting, means to interrupt workflows mid-run, and a path to unwind reversible actions—with honesty about those that cannot be reversed. Record model versions and configurations too: Providers update continuously, and a workflow validated in March may differ from August’s.

    Five workflows can be governed individually; 500 cannot. Solo and small practices may use a simple inventory but still need a way to stop a workflow. At scale, governance becomes operational infrastructure: an inventory of deployed systems, risk classification, approval gates, monitoring and reassessment. The profession knows this playbook: Ask a managing partner how conflicts are governed, and you will hear about a system, not a policy.

    Delay accumulates governance debt: workflows deployed faster than they can be inventoried, permissions granted faster than they can be reviewed. Like all debt, it compounds quietly. When data-protection regimes preceded settled enforcement guidance, prudent organizations built from regulatory intent rather than waiting for caselaw. Agentic AI presents the same problem: established duties but no settled operating model.

    Sources indicate that ownership, calibrated oversight, permission limits, traceability, reversibility and governance at scale matter wherever organizations deploy agentic AI. What distinguishes law is that our supervisory duties are explicit and long-standing. We are not a special case. We are an early test case.

    According to recent reports, fortunately, the test is familiar. Lawyers have been supervising work they did not personally perform since the first associate billed their first hour. The question is no longer only whether lawyers can use AI competently. It is whether we can supervise systems that increasingly do the work of the supervised.

    Sources indicate that scott A. Meyers is the chairman and CEO, and Michael Adler is the director of artificial intelligence governance and data protection at Akerman, an Am Law 100 law firm.

    It has been revealed that editor’s Note: In preparing the content, the authors used generative AI tools under their direction and supervision and provide the following description of the manner and extent of that use. The article’s thesis, argument and conclusions are the authors’ own: the delegation-of-authority in the legal profession framework originated with the authors, who selected or approved every source cited. Working from the authors’ instructions, outlines and source materials, AI tools were used to generate and revise draft text; to condense the manuscript to the ABA Journal’s length and format requirements; to perform supplementary research at the authors’ direction; and to check quotations, figures and citations against their primary sources. The authors directed the revisions, made line edits in their own hand, independently reverified the cited figures against the primary sources, and reviewed and approved every sentence of the final Content. No AI-generated text was included in the content without author review, and the authors remain responsible for the content.

    According to recent reports, mind Your Business is a series of columns written by lawyers, legal professionals and others within the legal industry. The purpose of these columns is to offer practical guidance for attorneys on how to run their practices, provide information about the latest trends in legal technology and how it can help lawyers work more efficiently, and strategies for building a thriving business.

    The top five Watsons (read: “often impressed best friend narrators”) in crime fiction

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (716 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, I don’t mean this literally, I mean this professionally.
    • That’s what Watson DOES in the Sherlock Holmes series.
    • Assembled for your reading pleasure are five series that follow this general formula: brilliant detective, awed chronicler.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Every great detective needs a Watson.

    In a recent development, I don’t mean this literally, I mean this professionally. By “Watson,” I refer to the archetype of the Very Impressed Best Friend And Narrator. A hype man who also tells the story. A deputy who keeps going “wow, look at this guy” as he tells you about this guy. Bonus points if he’s also this guy’s roommate.

    That’s what Watson DOES in the Sherlock Holmes series. He’s a carnival barker and a nonfiction writer. Sherlock Holmes is not only his friend, he’s also his subject. Watson isn’t only HIS best friend, he’s also his audience. But he’s also his publicist. He‘s fascinated by Holmes, and he knows tons of people will also be fascinated by Holmes. His job is PR, and man does he do it well.

    Assembled for your reading pleasure are five series that follow this general formula: brilliant detective, awed chronicler.

    Watson: Archie Goodwin  Detective: Nero Wolfe.

    Sources indicate that in the beloved Rex Stout series, the young Archie Goodwin narrates AND does all the legwork for the affluent, grouchy, high-on-the-horse bibliophile and private detective Nero Wolfe (who hates leaving his luxurious brownstone). Archie, a handsome and dapper young man, is a quick-witted, fast-talking factotum. And he’s always pretty impressed with the mental calculations of his sedentary boss.

    Watson: S.S. Van Dine Detective: Philo Vance.

    According to recent reports, S.S. Van Dine takes the Watson gambit even further than Watson does. S.S. Van Dine is a real person, the real-life writer of the Philo Vance books (though “S.S. Van Dine” was a pen name; his real name was Willard Huntington Wright), who writes himself into the stories as the best friend of the brilliant, suave, dandyish detective Philo Vance. Here, he’s not Vance’s creator, merely his chronicler, and the two solve innumerable mysteries together during the Jazz Age.

    Watson: Unnamed  Detective: C. Auguste Dupin.

    We don’t know the name of the guy who narrates his friend and roommate Auguste Dupin’s feats of investigation, but he is really the OG Watson. They meet at various rare booksellers and eventually hit it off, becoming pals and then deciding to move in together. And then the unnamed narrator marvels as Dupin solves crimes, sometimes after hitting the scene of the crime, sometimes without leaving their house.

    Recent findings suggest that watson: Capt. Arthur Hastings  Detective: Hercule Poirot.

    Hercule Poirot’s best friend Arthur Hastings doesn’t narrate ALL the Poirot stories (he narrates eight of thirty-three novels, and twenty-one of fifty-one short stories), because, after Hastings meets a beautiful music hall performer half his age in Murder on the Links, he marries her and eventually moves with her to South America, where they have four kids. But Hastings still appears, sprinkled throughout the Poirot canon, because he returns to England for business a lot. So they get together and crime-solve then.

    Watson: Anthony Horowitz Detective: Daniel Hawthorne.

    In a recent development, look, I’d have such a soft spot for Anthony Horowitz even WITHOUT the these books, simply because I grew up reading the Alex Rider series. But the Horowitz and Hawthorne mysteries, in which “Horowitz himself” tags along as the sidekick and narrator (he’s NOT ONLY the Watson, here, but also the Van Dine), are so delightful. I love these guys. Their work is very collaborative (and these books are sneaky, since Hawthorne isn’t the real mastermind, but Horowitz himself). And often, they’re at odds. But that’s fine. This subgenre loves nuance. Horowitz is a Watson with his own (even more impressive) list of mystery bona-fides than his subject, which is what makes this series even more interesting.

    Sara Paretsky on inventing languages and feeling kinship with older characters

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2371 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that for more than four decades, V.I.
    • Paretsky’s newest book, Bad Manufacturer, introduces a protagonist more in line with her age: Lily Sedaka, a former CIA field agent now in her seventies.
    • Paretsky will continue writing novels about Warshawski, but this upcoming character will enable the author to tap into her own lived experiences—complete with the aches and pains that come with age.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that for more than four decades, V.I. Warshawski, the fictional private investigator created by Sara Paretsky, has aged slowly. In her late twenties and early thirties in the first novels, Warshawski is now about fifty years old. Unfortunately for Paretsky and the rest of us, time has flown by at a normal pace. In her mid-thirties when she published her first novel, Indemnity Only, in 1982, Paretsky is now seventy-nine and has less in common with her more youthful character.

    Paretsky’s newest book, Bad Manufacturer, introduces a protagonist more in line with her age: Lily Sedaka, a former CIA field agent now in her seventies. The book marks her twenty-fifth novel and the first non-Warshawski novel since Ghost Country in 1998.

    Paretsky will continue writing novels about Warshawski, but this upcoming character will enable the author to tap into her own lived experiences—complete with the aches and pains that come with age.

    Industry observers note that like her Warshawski novels, Bad Company takes place in Chicago but with an added worldview. Sections are set in the fictional Central Asian country of Hayalistan, where Sedaka once was stationed. In an interview conducted over Zoom, Paretsky reflected on the decision to introduce a new character and the difficulty that came with inventing a language.

    L. Wayne Hicks: I wanted to ask you what made you decide to unveil a new character after so much success with the V.I. Warshawski novels.

    Recent findings suggest that sara Paretsky: Oh, you know, it wasn’t a deliberate decision. But she came to me. I was on vacation in Paris, which makes me sound more glamorous than I am. But especially because what happened was that I fell out of bed, which is totally not glamorous. And as I was rubbing my sore hip, I was thinking, what would happen if V.I. got to be my age, seventy-something, and injured herself and could no longer race around the streets after bad guys? And then I thought, I really don’t want V.I. to be old and creaky. I want her to stay kind of fifty-ish.

    And really, in that moment, Lily came to me with her name, Lily, this ex-CIA agent who now was on the run from the CIA. The whole storyline took years to develop, and many false starts, but that was how it happened.

    LWH: Is Lily going to be a recurring character?

    Industry observers note that SP: I hope so. You know, everything depends on my being able to write faster than I do because I’m under contract to do a latest book in the V.I. series. I wrote 10,000 words that I threw out. I wrote ten thousand more words and threw out eight thousand. But I’ve started a file on Lily. I have a storyline that I’m really excited about for her that is totally hers. It’s not the kind of thing V.I. would be involved with.

    LWH: I was wondering since Lily and V.I are both in Chicago, whether there’d ever be a crossover or meetup.

    According to recent reports, SP: That’s a delicate question. I don’t know if I should say this or not. I mean, I don’t know if this is politically advisable to say this, but Disney owns the rights in perpetuity to V.I. and any characters that hover around her. So, I want to own Lily, and that means that much as I would like to have a lot of crossover, that’s just not going to happen.

    LWH: Okay, and Disney has the rights because of the movie? (The 1991 film V.I. Warshawski, starring Kathleen Turner.).

    It has been revealed that SP: Yes, exactly. And I was young, ignorant, relied on advice. It wasn’t great advice, and here I am.

    Recent findings suggest that LWH: Do you feel more of a kinship to Lily than you do to V.I. since you’re both in your seventies?

    SP: When V.I. and I were the same age, I don’t think I felt a kinship with her. I was thinking about that this morning. I have a cousin who’s my age, whom I admire greatly. I love her. She’s a wonderful woman in every way. She’s kind of more like V.I. She just got back from backpacking, carrying a thirty-pound backpack through the Boundary Waters in northern Minnesota, and she’s done many wonderful things in her life for women, so I admire her and I admire V.I. in that way.

    But I have to say that I actually actively envy Lily. I would like to be Lily. I never wanted to be V.I. I’d like to be that person who could insert herself into groups the way she did when she was actively working as a CIA agent. She scampers up and down mountains. She bathes naked with local women under the full moon and the glacier waters in the country where she worked.

    Industry observers note that and I mean, like V.I., she takes a lot of risks, but unlike V.I., she’s a team player to a certain extent, insofar as the CIA lets her have a team, and then she’s got these incredible linguistic gifts, so I would like to be Lily, whereas I don’t want to be my cousin. I just like to admire my cousin.

    LWH: And you had to create an entirely fictional country for Lily to have had her adventures in.

    SP: Yes, I realized if I was going to write a book that was set in the CIA world, sort of set in the CIA world, if I wrote about any of the things that the CIA has really been involved with, I would spend the rest of my life answering letters from people who stated, “Well, you got this detail on, and I was there from 1950 to 1990,” and so I thought, okay, the way around that is to create my own country, and then created my own language.

    That was a mistake because when the audio recorder was doing the reading, they said there are sixty words in the Hayali language that are in the book that they needed to know how to pronounce. And I’m looking at them and thinking, why did I create a language that was Qs, Zs, and Ws? I don’t know how to pronounce these words. Figure it out yourself. But anyway, I made a stab at it, and I thought, well, if I ever do that again, it’s going to be a language that looks like French.

    LWH: You could have made Lily a retired CIA agent who doesn’t have a lot of health problems. She doesn’t have a bum shoulder. But you gave her things that people in their seventies would be going through. Is that just to make it more realistic?

    It has been revealed that SP: Well, yes, and you know it’s sort of a reflection of my own lived experience. I feel lucky to be in as good shape as I am with eighty kind of lurking around the corner, but I was badly injured in a car crash some years ago, and I have residual problems that keep me from scampering up and down mountains, and I just think if you get to be my age and you don’t have arthritis or joint problems or something that’s slowing you down, you have lived a lucky life.

    Recent findings suggest that so, I wanted that lived experience to be something that people could relate to as much as I relate to it, or in the same way that I relate to it. We all have these issues that we’re dealing with, and yet people carry on. And I think that was what I wanted to do with Lily to show that you can just keep on keeping on, even when it’s not so easy.

    Sources indicate that LWH: When you started writing the V.I. series, you and she were roughly about the same age, but you’ve made her age a lot slower than the rest of us mortals.

    Recent findings suggest that SP: Right. It’s just one of her superpowers. I had no imagination about what that series would be. I didn’t know it was going to be a series. I wanted to create a woman detective who was sort of turning the tables on the standard roles for women in crime fiction forty-plus years ago.

    According to recent reports, I thought I would write this book and then I would go back to whatever else I was doing in my life, which at that time was selling computers to insurance agents. I don’t know if I would have made different decisions if I’d imagined that there would be twenty-three more books about V.I. coming down the pike.

    I’m not sure when you’re thirty that you can imagine seventy. I looked at my mother who had terrible health challenges. She was in her fifties then, and I thought, oh well, you know, it’s just a question of taking care of yourself. And then I got to be fifty and had my own issues. Life gives you these slaps in the face to tell you to stop being so arrogant.

    LWH: Why do you think it was important to have Lily suffering from some of the physical ailments that she does versus making her full of vim and vigor and in great physical shape?

    Recent findings suggest that SP: Well, I want a character who readers can connect to. I think everyone second-guesses themselves. Everyone makes choices that they may look back on with regret, as Lily does. She’s thinking back over her long life of service and realizing that there were things that she just didn’t see. They were going on in front of her and she didn’t see them.

    I hope people can see their own experience in her, even if their experiences are, I don’t know, in a small town in the Midwest, as opposed to hiking up and down mountains in Central Asia. They’ll see that fundamentally she’s the same kind of person they are and if she can achieve her aspirations, other people can achieve their own aspirations.

    LWH: What can you do with a the character in her seventies that you couldn’t or wouldn’t be able to do with with V.I.?

    SP: One reason that I took a break from V.I. was that she was getting to be too much like me. Too worried, too feeling overwhelmed by responsibility, too much questioning her judgment. V.I. is supposed to be a lot more—I don’t know if carefree is the right word, but bold. V.I. is supposed to be bolder.

    Lily is effective, but she’s not bold in that way. She’s someone who is more emotionally akin to me, I would say. And I was letting V.I. get too much into that space, and it was—I don’t want to say destroying her as a character, but it was making her character less what I wanted her to be. Bringing Lily on board and letting her have that part of my emotional landscape now makes it possible to have V.I revert more to what should be her character.

    LWH: Does Lily being as old as she is make her sort of invisible to people and let her go about her skullduggery or whatever she needs to get done?

    SP: Yes. There is no disguise like being an old woman in America. I’ll tell you one of the things that I loved about Grace and Frankie in the first episode with Lily Tomlin and Jane Fonda, is they’re in a liquor store and they cannot get the attention of the person behind the counter because he’s talking to some young person and he just doesn’t register two old women and so they shoplift. It’s like: why not?

    According to recent reports, LWH: There are going to be readers who read that Sara Peretsky has a new novel out, but they might be upset that it’s not another V.I. story. Do you think there’s going to be appeal, that people are going to enjoy reading both characters, both series?

    Sources indicate that SP: Well, I hope so. I mean, I’ve had very good feedback from the people who read the book so far. It was published September twenty-four in England. They usually publish the same month as my American publishers, but for some reason they were two months ahead or six weeks ahead. But they sold out their first printing the first week it was on sale, so that that’s encouraging that English readers were willing to take the chance on a new character.

    LWH: There are many novelists who have died but their characters keep going. Robert Parker, his Spenser novels are still being written by other people, but Sue Grafton mentioned no, the alphabet ends with Y. What is your thinking? What is your preference?

    SP: Oh, I’m with Sue on that. You know, this is my voice. This is my presence in the world. V.I. is too much part of my life, and I feel the same way about Lily. There are other people who write better than I do. There are other people who write faster, more creatively, but it wouldn’t be my voice.

    Years ago, the Japanese took over the Macallan whisky organization. I was talking to one of the master distillers in the Highlands, and he remarked that that Suntory was bringing him over to be their lead tester on their chemically created version of Highland whisky, and he said, “They have the Scottish water, they have the Scottish peat, they have the Scottish barley, but they don’t have the Scottish air, and it is not Scotch.”.

    That’s how I feel about my character. You might have the storyline, you might have the name, but you don’t have my spirit, and so it is not V.I.

    L. Wayne Hicks is a freelance writer who covered real-life crimes for newspapers in Florida and Colorado, and has written profiles of many mystery writers including Sara Paretsky, Michael Connelly, John Dunning, Donald J. Sobol, and Stephen White.
